Performance was measured using sentence-level label-surface matching with relaxed and exact-surface F1. Results: The highest zero-shot relaxed F1 was 0.337, compared with 0.836-0.841 for the BERT baselines. At the larger output limits, all eight fine-tuned LLMs with at least 13B total parameters exceeded both BERT baselines (relaxed F1, 0.882-0.914; exact-surface F1, 0.840-0.880). Across three-seed means, increasing the output limit improved relaxed F1 by 0.052-0.085, alongside higher recall and fewer length-limited outputs. JSON Schema constraints changed relaxed F1 by -0.014 to +0.008 among seven models outside the two reasoning-oriented configurations, while medical-general model pairs showed no consistent advantage for medical specialization. Conclusions: On this historical Japanese case-report benchmark, task-specific fine-tuning combined with adequate generation capacity was associated with stronger LLM extraction performance. Output-token limits materially affected comparisons with BERT, whereas enforcing output structure alone did not overcome low zero-shot accuracy.
authors: Feng Han, Ayako Yagahara, Kenji Hirata

title: EGS: A Complementary Safety Framework for Educational LLMs
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer strong potential for personalized education, but adolescent-facing deployment raises risks of toxic, biased, misleading, or developmentally inappropriate content. We argue that educational safety should move beyond binary refusal: student queries are often ambiguous or curiosity-driven, requiring contextual guidance rather than simple blocking. We introduce the Educational Guardrail System (EGS), a lightweight, model-agnostic runtime framework that complements intrinsic alignment through query moderation, scenario-aware pedagogical guidance, and response moderation. EGS triages inputs by risk level, redirects gray-zone queries with category-specific educational interventions, and audits outputs before delivery. Experiments across general and education-specific benchmarks show that EGS improves moderation performance, refusal quality, and jailbreak robustness across diverse LLMs. These findings suggest that defense-in-depth guardrails can strengthen safety while preserving the pedagogical utility required in educational LLMs. Our code and model weights will be publicly available to support community adoption.
authors: Zexuan Fei, Zhengnan Guo, Yiming Luo

title: RISA: Recoverable Sparse Attention for Block-Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Block-wise diffusion language models (DLMs) refine multiple tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. Their long-context inference, however, remains bottlenecked by memory-bound attention: every denoising step repeatedly reads a growing historical key--value (KV) cache. Directly applying sparse attention does not fully solve this problem, because different queries can select different pages, inflating the block's collective read set, while repeated support construction adds overhead and permanent eviction can discard information needed later. We present RISA, a recoverable sparse-attention method with shared read plans for block-wise DLMs. RISA exploits the fact that historical KV remains fixed within a block while queries evolve across denoising steps. Newly generated history is organized into exact priority and recovery tiers; seed queries then build a protected, bounded read plan whose indices are reused across the block while attention is recomputed with fresh queries and current-block KV. This separates history preservation from repeated reading and amortizes sparse-support construction without changing the backbone or decoder. On DreamReasoner-8B, RISA retains comparable task performance. At 32K, the default configuration speeds up attention by $2.67\times$ and fixed-trajectory requests by $1.36\times$ over dense, and attention speedup reaches $5.53\times$ at 128K. Across eight settings on three models, RISA decodes faster than the tested MAGE, QUEST, and LoSA budgets at matched KL.
authors: Xinrui Zhong, Fanjiang Ye, Yuke Wang

title: From Imperfective Paradox to Moorean Absurdity: Single-Chain Reasoning Lock-In and Multi-Candidate Verbalization Across Aspectual and Pragmatic Ambiguity
abstract: Natural language entailment and coherence judgments often depend on whether an event merely occurred, reached a telic culmination, satisfied a plan, or was evaluated under multiple pragmatic standards. We test observable consequences of the single-chain premature lock-in hypothesis across four preregistered, sealed formal experiments on Qwen3-8B-Q8_0 (16,640 formal units, temperature=0.0): 15 of 16 hypothesis slots retain confirmatory status (12 rejecting H0 under within-experiment Holm control at alpha_fam=0.05; E3_H3 demoted to descriptive status). In Experiment 1, Direct-CoT vs. MCU differs by 25.00 pp on telic high-confidence completion (Holm p=1.31239e-05), while NLI-CoT collapses by -91.25 pp on uninterrupted atelic items (Holm p=1.81805e-21). Multi-Candidate Verbalization (MCV) elicits K=5 weighted estimates in one call, separating the prompt from unweighted (MCU) and self-weighted (MCW) readouts. Mandarin (E2) and English (E3) expose an Interruption-Anchored Realis Paradox under NLI-CoT. In Experiment 4, MCU-CF raises perceived coherence on implicit Moorean sentences by 26.64 pp over Direct-CoT (Holm p=0.0006), alongside Direct-CF - Direct-CoT = 29.15 pp and MCU-CoT - Direct-CoT = 17.31 pp. A 1,800-call OpenAI ablation and a stage="dev" P16.7 cross-model extension (4,240 planned/collected units across five external models: 4,222 valid, 18 format-missing, 0 transport-missing; <2% missing per slice; OpenAI gpt-4o-mini at top_logprobs=20 achieves 1,000/1,000 valid units) show that discrete NLI-CoT and scalar Direct-CoT judgments dissociate across models. Confirmatory effects concern observable prompt-and-readout protocols; internal premature lock-in remains a hypothesis. All code, stimuli, preregistered analysis plans, and verification tools are available at https://github.com/asj252/llm-judgment-studies.
authors: An-Sheng Jhang

title: Is 4-Bit Quantization More Than Noise to a Chat Model's Safety Behaviour? Attributing Behavioural Shifts with Matched Perturbations
abstract: Chat models on phones and laptops are usually 4-bit copies of the model that was evaluated, and audits of such copies disagree about what quantization does to refusal. A 4-bit build is one of many weight perturbations of the same size, so a change in its behaviour could come from its specific rounding error or from any perturbation that large. In a pre-registered study of three 3-4B chat models, with paired tests, blind human labels and an 8-bit null, we find two 4-bit shifts of opposite sign: with a compliant reply prefilled, Qwen2.5-3B continues into harmful content more often, and on held-out jailbreaks Llama-3.2-3B complies 10.3 points less often. Matched perturbations separate the two. Shuffled and Gaussian versions of the error average close to zero, while scaling the real error, from its mirror image to twice its size, changes behaviour near-linearly. At half the real error, Llama's likelihood is almost unchanged, yet it already complies 5.8 points less often, and llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, at the same bits per weight, moves neither model. Refusal under 4-bit quantization depends on the specific rounding error, not on bits per weight or likelihood, so each build has to be compared with its original.
authors: Ege Kaya

title: What RL on Expert-Built Tasks Teaches Nemotron 3.5 Super
abstract: We post-train NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super (120B total, 12B active parameters) with reinforcement learning (RL) on five expert-built task datasets, one at a time: real-world software engineering, complex constraints, long-horizon tool use, professional chart understanding and enterprise document reasoning. Each run trains a fresh rank-32 LoRA adapter with CISPO on Tinker, with no supervised stage, and each adapter is compared with the base model on the same tasks, harness and settings. On twelve headline benchmarks, eight built by other groups and four by Surge AI, the gains range from +4.5 points on IFBench to +13.8 on GDP_pdf, which rises from 10.4% to 24.2%; SWE-bench Pro V2 rises from 86.9% to 92.1%, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 63.9% to 70.3%, MultiChallenge from 58.3% to 66.6%, AutomationBench from 14.8% to 27.5% and Chartography from 39.4% to 50.6%. The document adapter, trained without API tools, also gains +8.0 points on AutomationBench. In attempts read side by side with the base model's on tasks each adapter newly solves, the base model's failures recur in a few modes, and each adapter does more often what the base model missed: the tool-use adapter finds the data and the rules before acting, the coding adapter writes its own test or scratch files on SWE-bench Pro V2, the constraints adapter carries earlier turns into its answers, the chart adapter measures the marks in code, and the document adapter reads AutomationBench's spreadsheets.
authors: Sushant Mehta, Edwin Chen

title: Lexical Tone and Word Order Matter in Translation: Prosodic Correspondence Across Languages
abstract: Prosody conveys emphasis, emotion, and intent, yet its correspondence across translation remains underexplored, especially when languages differ in lexical tone and word order. To our knowledge, we present the first systematic word-level analysis of prosodic correspondence in translated speech spanning tonal and non-tonal Asian languages, with comparisons to European-language findings and explicit analyses of lexical tone and word reordering. Building on prior evidence of fine-grained prosody correspondence in European-language pairs, we investigate how these linguistic factors relate to word-level pitch and energy correspondence between English and five languages: Mandarin Chinese, Thai, and Vietnamese, which have lexical tone, and Japanese and Korean as additional comparisons. Correspondence is generally lower than previously reported European-language estimates. Adjusting for lexical tone increases pitch correspondence for English-Mandarin Chinese, English-Thai, and English-Vietnamese. However, English-Japanese and English-Korean also exhibit lower correspondence than the European-language estimates, indicating that tonal status alone does not explain the observed pattern. Greater word reordering is associated with weaker local correspondence even under semantic alignment, suggesting that semantic alignment does not fully account for differences in prosodic organization. These findings characterize the limits of fine-grained acoustic correspondence across translation and motivate prosody modeling that accounts for lexical pitch constraints and the structural context of translated content.
authors: Haopeng Xie, Ismail Rasim Ulgen, Shengying Zhao

title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)
abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every issue the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.
authors: Allen G. Roush, Minh Nhat Nguyen, Ravid Shwartz-Ziv

title: What MoE Routing Controls: Causal Interventions on Expert Trajectories
abstract: In mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, a token is routed to a sequence of experts across layers. We investigate how forcing tokens onto chosen expert paths influences model behavior. We build a target path from the experts that a concept's or role's tokens most often use, and we add a fixed bias to each target expert's router logit during generation to steer the token toward this expert path. We study two kinds of targets. Format targets concern the form of the output, and concept targets concern its topic. In Qwen3-30B-A3B, we show that steering a format path changes the text the model writes. We also show that steering a concept path shifts the model's next-token probabilities toward the concept, even when the path is built in another language, yet this shift has little effect on the generated text. We investigate why formats reach the text but concepts do not by steering only part of the generation, and find evidence that a format, once started, reinforces itself. We show that the concepts religion and money steer most strongly, and that the effect is concentrated in the middle layers. We attempt to explain why the strength of the effect varies by concept through an analysis of embedding distinctiveness and word frequency.
authors: Mukund Athmaram, Manoj Rao, Liang Ma

title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.
authors: Hyunjong Ok, Jaeho Lee

title: Beyond Acuity Accuracy: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Patient-Facing Emergency Triage AI Tools
abstract: Patient-facing AI triage tools may support care-seeking and emergency department prioritization, but require evaluation beyond acuity accuracy alone. We developed SAFE-Triage, a framework integrating human review, automated metrics, LLM-as-judge evaluation, and simulation testing across clinical performance, patient interaction, and clinician-facing summary quality. We applied SAFE-Triage to 40 MIMIC-IV-derived emergency vignettes and a 10,030-case acuity analysis comparing prompted LLM triage (PLT) with rule-augmented prompted LLM triage (rPLT). PLT achieved higher emergency severity index (ESI) accuracy (57.5% vs 42.8%, $P < 0.001$), lower undertriage (13.1% vs 29.8%, $P < 0.001$), and higher clinician ratings across all domains. rPLT produced shorter and more stable outputs with higher automated readability scores. SAFE-Triage identified trade-offs between acuity accuracy, undertriage risk, communication quality, readability, and summary quality, supporting pre-deployment refinement and ongoing monitoring by showing where triage tools are efficient, need improvement, or need clinician oversight.
authors: Ruio Heerschap, Henry Foote, Mahmoud Alwakeel

title: RLDE: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Interpretable Iterative Document Editing
abstract: Improving the quality, clarity, and flow of long documents remains a challenging problem in NLP, as human editing typically occurs through iterative refinement rather than a single-pass rewrite. Most existing automated systems act as black-box generators or rely on supervised learning, limiting interpretability and failing to capture the sequential nature of revisions. In this paper, we propose RLDE, an automated end-to-end metric-driven RL framework that formulates document revision as a reference-free MDP problem (unsupervised with respect to paired document-revision targets). Working with a limited action space (NOOP, INSERT, DELETE, REPLACE), RLDE leverages Pointer Networks for dynamic span selection at the token level and sends generative actions to the frozen BART-base model to obtain context-aware suggestions. PPO agents learn to optimize a multi-objective reward function based on readability, perplexity, and grammar metrics with the help of a novel SBERT-based Semantic Preservation Penalty constraint to avoid deletion degeneracy. Evaluations on the BEA-2019 dataset showed statistically significant results (p < 0.01) across all metrics, where Flesch Reading Ease increased from 49.8 to 59.4, perplexity decreased from 63.7 to 39.8, while preserving 93% of semantic information. When compared to Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompt-engineered models like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2, RLDE shows high performance at a very low computational inference cost. Moreover, the quality of edits generated by RLDE has been verified via human evaluations, scoring 4.9/5 for meaning preservation and 4.4/5 for edit quality.
authors: Nikhil Parkar, M. Marimuthu, Riya Joshi

title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.
authors: Adi Krishnamoorthy, X. Y. Han

title: GauntletScore: Auditable Fact-Checking That Matches the Best Published Checkers on LLM-AggreFact
abstract: Checking whether a generated sentence is supported by its source document is a standard safeguard for AI-written text, and the strongest published checkers are single models. We describe GauntletScore, an evidence engine whose few rules and thresholds were set on the benchmark's development split. It puts typed questions to independent readers from different providers and records each answer as a measurement in an evidence ledger. It combines the measurements with a fixed Bayesian rule that counts a contradiction only when two readers agree. On the full LLM-AggreFact test split (29,320 claims across 11 datasets), following the leaderboard's approach, GauntletScore achieves 79.51 balanced accuracy, above every average published on the leaderboard as of 15 November 2026. That places it level with the best of them, nimble-v4-max (79.45 from its published dataset scores; the engine's 95% interval, 78.47 to 80.53, contains it). On the same claims it beats two of its three readers used alone (Readers A and B) by 1.66 and 2.17 points (95% intervals 0.80 to 2.53 and 1.29 to 3.06). Without AggreFact-CNN, described below, the leads are 0.90 and 1.32 and both intervals stay above zero. The engine also records the evidence behind every verdict, which a single model does not. Its largest margin is on full-length news articles checked against multi-sentence summaries (AggreFact-CNN), a format that resembles much regulated writing. There it scores 76.45, the best on the leaderboard, against 70.1 for the next best and 63.9 to 67.8 for the six systems with the highest averages. The test split was run once, on an engine frozen before the first test claim, under a stopping plan committed in advance. We release per-claim predictions and the scoring script.
authors: Ernie Hobbs, Jim Hinson

title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.
authors: Gengyue Dong, Ye Wei, Zheng Zhu

title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information upfront and assess only the final diagnosis or rationale. This setup ignores the need to acquire diagnostic evidence incrementally from incomplete information in real-world diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiagTrace, a source-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reconstruct the documented diagnostic trajectory through interactive information seeking. Each benchmark instance is built from a PubMed Central case report and includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references. DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties, with 225 used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency. Results reveal trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.
authors: Yufan Wang, Rui Yang, Yi Lin

title: Large Language Models as Nonlinear Dynamical Systems: The Three Clocks of Depth, Training, and Generation
abstract: Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.
authors: Maor Farid

title: Modeling Document and Section Hierarchies in Embedding Space
abstract: Embedded topic models integrate word embeddings into the topic generation process, producing coherent topics and robust performance on large vocabularies. However, each document is represented by a single topic distribution, ignoring its internal structure. Many real world collections, including legal documents, company and government reports, and online discussion forums, exhibit hierarchical organization in which documents consist of multiple sections that often address distinct subtopics. We introduce the Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model (hETM), a structured topic model that couples the topic distribution of a document and those of its sections through a hierarchical prior in the embedding space. We derive an amortized variational inference procedure for hETM and evaluate it on structured collections from each of these domains. Experimental results show that hETM achieves the lowest or near-lowest held-out perplexity among flat and hierarchical topic model baselines, along with comparable or higher topic quality. It also performs strongly on a downstream clustering task, achieving the best clustering performance on most of the collections.
authors: Kriste Krstovski, Sharyn O'Halloran, Kshitij Chandna

title: Beyond Bitwidth: Deployment-Constrained Mixed-Precision Quantization for Multilingual LLM Inference on NVIDIA Blackwell
abstract: Low-bit LLM quantization is useful only if a model preserves service-relevant accuracy, executes through supported GPU kernels, and meets measured memory and latency limits. We study Qwen3-8B on NVIDIA B200 with vLLM, including INT2/INT3, GPTQ, NVFP4, and mixed-precision configurations. We verify native packed execution and precision on all 144 fused linear modules and evaluate Korean, English, numerical, and reasoning quality under preregistered gates. Packed INT2 and INT3 execute, but all seven tested INT2 grids degenerate on generation. Isolated module-restoration effects are strongly non-additive; Korean and reasoning sensitivity rankings disagree, and a promising INT4/INT8 development candidate fails independent final evaluation. A configuration with 16-bit activations, 98 NVFP4 weight-only modules, 46 INT8 modules, and an INT8 output head passes all gates on the untouched FINAL-81 set (5,168 items): 5.917 GiB of weight-loading memory (limit 5.98), Korean teacher-correct retention 0.904 (gate 0.90), and TPOT ratio 0.939 relative to BF16. It improves paired accuracy over NVFP4 W4A4 by +1.4 percentage points (Bonferroni-adjusted interval [+0.2, +2.6]), compared with +3.4 points on the selection set. This comparison changes both activation precision and INT8 protection; exploratory analyses suggest that the activation change contributes substantially, but the isolated allocation effect is not established. Final checkpoints were not retained, and bitwise rebuild reproducibility remains unverified.
authors: Hyojung Han

title: It's My Turn! Interpretable Methods Reveal Developmental Differences from Mother-Child Conversational Dynamics
abstract: Understanding conversational interactions between mothers and children is an important challenge for computational behavioral modeling. Existing methods use traditional statistical approaches and subjective measures of conversational dynamics, without incorporating temporal or probabilistic modeling. We developed an interpretable computational framework that combines sequence analysis, information-theoretic measures, and Bayesian hierarchical modeling to characterize temporal conversational dynamics in parent-child play. We applied this framework to interactions from 94 mother-child dyads with two-year-old children. Sequence analysis revealed that dyads with lower language development (as defined by scores on the Bayley developmental test) exhibited more heterogeneous conversational organization and fewer serve-and-return exchanges than higher-development dyads, a reciprocal turn-taking pattern in which one partner initiates communication and the other responds. Mutual information analyses suggested differences in conversational predictability between lower- and higher-development dyads, although the bootstrap confidence intervals overlapped. Bayesian hierarchical models estimated temporal trajectories for maternal consecutive turns, child responses following maternal speech, and overlapping responses; HDIs showed that trajectories differed in whether they excluded 0, but there were no statistically credible differences between the Bayley groups. Overall, these results indicate that children with higher developmental scores have more organized and predictable communication styles, with more ``serve-and-return" patterns with their mothers. These results demonstrate that interpretable computational representations of conversational dynamics capture developmental differences beyond simple measures of speech quantity.
authors: A'di Dust, Anura Deshpande, Pat Levitt

title: Solver to System: LLM Reasoning Across Representations and Execution in Scientific Simulation
abstract: Simulators based on partial differential equations (PDEs) are widely used to model physical systems, but generating and interpreting PDE solver code with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging. Scientific simulation code is a useful testbed for LLM scientific reasoning because (1) one system can be represented by code, equations, natural language, and numerical trajectories and (2) code can execute successfully while implementing invalid physics. We introduce Solver2System, a dataset of PDE solvers with multiple representations, controlled corruptions, and lexical perturbations, to evaluate whether LLMs can recover the underlying physical system through (1) cross-representation consistency and (2) static and agentic detection of physical invalidity. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and lexical perturbations to code alter interpretation of other unchanged representations. Execution improves physical-validity judgments, but weaker agents can judge correctly without identifying the causal defect. Thus, LLMs may reach correct judgments despite inconsistent representation reconciliation or causal misdiagnosis.
authors: Eliza Berman, Rohan Subramanian, Shreya Jha

title: Conserved Verdicts, Drifting Commitments: Identifying Harmful Overthinking
abstract: A reasoning model that has reached a correct answer can lose it by continuing to think. Deciding whether to stop means comparing two probabilities at the same point of a chain: that the answer the model would give if stopped now is correct (its commitment), and that the answer it will finish with is correct (its verdict). We show that the verdict alone, which is what final-correctness probes estimate, cannot make this comparison. As a forecast of a fixed outcome it has no predictable drift, whether continuing helps or hurts. The commitment-verdict gap equals the expected remaining change in answer quality and the accuracy gained by stopping. A second identity splits any accuracy-versus-budget curve into answer change within chains and change in which chains are still running. We measure both on MATH-500. At all 379 points where DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B holds a correct answer, selected without regard to how its chain ends, continuing loses 3.6 points on average (95% CI [2.2, 5.2]), and the loss concentrates in a few problems. In six reasoning models from three families, on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench and with budgets up to 16,384 tokens, declining accuracy curves come from which chains remain, while the chains still reasoning keep or improve their answers. An oracle stopping rule gains at most +1.8 and +2.5 points at 1.5B and 7B. The framework says what to measure before building a stopping rule.
authors: Jianghong Zhou, Hao Rong, Chen Lin

title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding
abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.
authors: Jameson Sandler, Shane Bergsma, Mostafa Elhoushi

title: Latent Fact Composition under Next-Token Training
abstract: Controlled studies of latent two-hop reasoning train transformers to predict only the answer, whereas language models are trained to predict every token. We ask whether a model trained on every token learns to answer two-hop questions whose intermediate entity appears in no two-hop training example. We build a synthetic corpus with such questions. On this corpus every term of the loss can be computed exactly. A looped transformer, a standard transformer and DiscoLoop answer almost none of these questions. We therefore introduce the Baton family of looped transformers. They pass the intermediate entity to the second loop as a token embedding. When trained to predict only the answer, two of its three variants answer these questions almost perfectly. We then relate the success and failure of each model to three design conditions. Experiments that change one condition at a time agree with this hypothesis. When Baton is trained on every token, however, its accuracy on these questions rises and then declines. We further split the gradient of the next-token loss into three terms. Removing the two terms that depend on the particular training set raises the peak accuracy but does not remove the decline. The decline arises in the second hop while the model still recalls both facts.
authors: Tianyi Zhang, Feiying Chen

title: Call-Efficient ICD-10 Code Prediction via Supervised Candidate Generation and Selective LLM Invocation
abstract: Automatic assignment of ICD-10 codes from short clinical diagnosis text is a practical medical text classification and normalization task. The task is difficult because diagnosis phrases are short and noisy, the ICD-10 label space is hierarchical, and the class distribution is strongly imbalanced. This paper presents a call-efficient ICD-10 code prediction pipeline that combines transformer embeddings, tree-based supervised candidate generation, candidate-level reranking, and a gated LLM assistance. The evaluation uses a leakage-safe validation protocol: model and threshold selection are based on out-of-fold cross-validation predictions, while final reporting is performed on a locked test set with no shared source-file groups. The supervised conditional parent-code candidate generator reaches 74.32% Top-1 accuracy on the locked test set and 93.05% Top-10 candidate coverage. A direct zero-shot GPT-5.6-Sol baseline reaches 81.01% Top-1 accuracy, but requires an invocation of this large model for every diagnosis. The final deployable system, Pre-LLM fusion, reaches 81.24% OOF-CV accuracy and 83.19% locked-test accuracy while calling the LLM for only 31.97% of cases. This improves the locked-test error rate from 25.68% for the supervised parent-code baseline to 16.81%, corresponding to a 34.5% relative error reduction. The results show that the most effective role of the LLM is controlled reranking on uncertain examples rather than unrestricted coding or full-dataset invocation.
authors: Ilia Kopanichuk, Daniil Kartashev, Yuri Bolkonsky

title: Knowing Which, Not How Much: Language Models Order Party Positions They Cannot Place
abstract: Language models are increasingly asked where real actors stand: what a party's platform prioritises, what an institution has committed to. Such judgments are gradable, carrying both an order and a magnitude. Nearly every benchmark that tests them asks about one entity at a time, then reads that score as the model's knowledge of the domain. Order and magnitude, however, need not be acquired together. Text about social entities carries far more comparison than measurement, so a model may hold a dependable ordering with no anchored scale beneath it. We ask whether a model can place a documented social position on a scale or only order the actors it compares, and what that means for how such knowledge is measured. We test this on party positions in Japan and South Korea, where the Comparative Manifesto Project's coded data supplies a rare external answer key. Asked to order four parties, models beat the strongest fixed-answer baseline by more than a factor of two; asked to place one party on the same scale, they fall below it. The ordering survives inside those failed placements, and supplying the coded values lifts placement to near ceiling. Comparative and absolute questions about the same fact therefore measure different things here, and for party issue salience a benchmark built from one cannot speak for the other.
authors: Yousef Attia, Jarosław A. Chudziak

title: The Hidden Cost of MoE Diffusion Decoding: Profiling and Fixing the Sampler
abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) decode by iteratively denoising a full canvas of tokens, so every forward pass runs a per-token sampling and stopping pipeline over the entire canvas-by-vocabulary logits tensor. We profile single-user decoding of a 26B-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts model on a bandwidth-bound edge accelerator (NVIDIA GB10) and report a result that is easy to miss: after weight quantisation, this logits pipeline, not the expert GEMMs, is the single largest consumer of decode time. Unlike autoregressive decoding, where sampling touches one position's logits per committed token, diffusion decoding processes S times as many logit entries per output token, where S is the number of denoising steps. We show this pipeline is largely redundant or fusable and remove it in two lossless tiers: a bit-exact tier whose output is byte-identical to the reference decoder, and an accuracy-parity tier using a fused single-pass entropy kernel and Gumbel-max sampling. Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the full stack reaches 2.4-2.7 times end-to-end speedup over bf16 at unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH, on a single 273 GB/s device. We confirm the finding on a second, independently built diffusion MoE (LLaDA2.0-mini: pipeline 28.8% of decode, fused W4A16 3.3 times at accuracy parity) and show it disappears on a dense diffusion model (3.6%). The cost is specific to MoE diffusion, where quantisation makes the backbone cheap. Code and quantised weights are released.
authors: Harshit Samrat, Ramakrishna Paramahamsa Kompella

title: TUSI: A Citation-Grounded Graph-Based Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Persian Legal Question Answering
abstract: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in Persian law remains challenging because benchmarks lack realism, grounding, and coverage of legal reasoning. Existing resources are either synthetically generated from statutory texts, lacking natural information needs, or derived from informal legal question--answer sources without explicit linkage to authoritative legal documents, making them unsuitable for rigorous evaluation of grounded legal reasoning. To address this gap, we introduce TUSI-Bench, a structured Persian legal benchmark designed for the evaluation of RAG-based systems. TUSI-Bench is built upon a multi-layered legal knowledge framework containing 7,261 legal articles and integrating codified statutes, legal commentaries, doctrinal writings, and Supreme Court unification rulings. We also construct a legal knowledge graph linking articles and concepts for structure-aware retrieval. Based on this foundation, TUSI-Bench provides two complementary evaluation tasks: (i) TUSI-QA, an open-ended question answering benchmark containing 1,999 questions that requires grounded responses with explicit legal citations, and (ii) TUSI-Bar, a multiple-choice benchmark containing approximately 500 four-option questions derived from Iranian Bar examination questions. Furthermore, we propose a graph-based retrieval baseline that leverages relational structure within the legal knowledge graph. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating graph-based relations improves retrieval recall by up to 8 percentage points compared to standard baselines, highlighting the importance of structured legal representations for RAG systems. The proposed benchmark provides a standardized resource for evaluating grounded legal reasoning in Persian and enables future research on structured legal intelligence.
authors: Marzieh Karimi, Mehran Safayani, Alireza Basiri

title: SimAI: Mechanistic User Simulation through Psychological Network Models
abstract: Realistic user simulation enables the study of human interactions when direct experimentation is costly or potentially harmful. However, existing simulators largely overlook the psychological mechanisms that drive user behavior. We introduce SimAI, a framework for mechanistic user simulation that models how psychological factors interact to shape user responses. To overcome the challenge of supervising open-ended behavior, we propose a graph reconstruction objective that provides graph-level rewards based on how well simulated conversations reflect the underlying psychological relationships. To support this approach, we construct PSYCHE, a dataset of 18,576 profile-network pairs derived from 516 psychotherapy cases. Automatic evaluations show that SimAI achieves greater simulation and behavioral diversity than existing patient simulators while maintaining strong profile alignment. In an interactive study with 30 mental-health professionals and trainees, SimAI receives the highest average ratings for conversational authenticity, realistic help-seeking behavior, and clinical training utility. Beyond simulation quality, SimAI enables realistic clinical training and uncovers safety failures in prolonged AI interactions with vulnerable users. Code is available at https://github.com/behavioral-data/ANGEL-UserSim.
authors: Cheng Li, Adhyyan Narang, Jiayi Yuan

title: Corrupting Ties: Investigating Robustness to Bias Injection Across Multi-Agent Network Topologies
abstract: AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision-making contexts, where interactions among components can introduce fairness risks that remain undetected when auditing components or collective outcomes in isolation. As LLM-based multi-agent systems become more prevalent, understanding how biased information propagates through agent interactions is essential for assessing their fairness. We introduce a controlled bias injection framework that replaces selected agent responses with predefined biased ones, enabling an intervention-based analysis of how network topology and injection configurations shape system behavior. We propose decision divergence metrics that quantify the effects of these interventions at the agent, network, and system levels, and evaluate five topologies on three binary classification tasks using LLMs from the Qwen and Gemma families. Sequential networks show the greatest divergence, whereas fully connected and mesh networks show less. Injection position also matters: in star networks, injecting the central agent has larger effects than injecting peripheral agents. Models further differ in whether divergence follows the injected bias. These findings highlight the role of network structure in the propagation of biased information and motivate topology-aware auditing of fairness risks in multi-agent systems.
authors: Cléa Chataigner, Mina Arzaghi, Florian Carichon

title: Latent Lattice Language Models
abstract: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.
authors: Shivam Duggal, Zongze Wu, William T. Freeman

title: Quantifying the added value of human forecaster discussions for tropical cyclone intensity prediction
abstract: The National Hurricane Center routinely releases Tropical Cyclone Discussions that offer insights into its tropical cyclone forecasts. This study examines the added value of these discussions for intensity forecasting beyond a set of numerical predictors. For 637 Atlantic and eastern North Pacific tropical cyclones from the 2002-2023 hurricane seasons, we analyze the discussion text and its combination with 13 hurricane environmental predictors from SHIPS and ERA5 10-meter wind fields, for forecasting intensity changes at lead times of 24 to 120 hours using three modeling methods. In one approach, an end-to-end deep learning framework for the text shows that the discussions alone offer comparable value for 24-hour intensity forecasts to the SHIPS predictors. Adding discussion information to the SHIPS predictors in an ensemble of five such models reduces the mean absolute error of 24-hour maximum sustained wind forecasts for 2022-2023 cyclones from 9.89 to 8.90 kt, with a confidence interval that excludes zero when whole storms are resampled. The ERA5 wind fields have a minor effect on mean absolute error in wind predictions, and model rankings differ across predicted variables, lead times and model types. We provide prediction intervals for these forecasts, whose coverage falls below the 90% target during rapid intensification. Analysis of the text shows that words related to intensity and intensity change (such as intensify, weaken, eyewall and category) are important for the model predictions. This retrospective study shows the added value of the forecasters' discussions and suggests that multi-modal learning can help understand the predictive contribution of expert human judgment. The reanalysis data differ from real-time analyses, and the discussions are issued at least three hours after the valid time of the other inputs, so these results should not be interpreted operationally.
authors: Ilia Azizi, Frederick Iat-Hin Tam, Marc-Olivier Boldi

title: How VLMs Plan What's Next
abstract: When a vision-language model describes an image, it names one object at a time and it rarely repeats itself, yet how the model plans this order is far from obvious. We characterize the mechanism a VLM uses to decide where to look before it looks. The mechanism has four main parts. First, binding heads match the relevant text tokens against the image and resolve them into pointers to the matched image region. Second, the same binding heads bind each written answer to the region it came from, and the model turns it into a progress signal: a cursor, the position in the image up to which the list has been written. Third, a select step chooses the nearest unwritten region after the cursor, or stops. Finally, gaze heads execute the chosen pointer and return a concept of what is drawn there, which language heads and the late MLPs turn into a word in the language of the question. We validate each part of this mechanism through causal patching in Qwen3-VL models on a synthetic visual retrieval task, and test our mechanisms against alternative hypotheses. We further show that the mechanism holds across input formats, natural photographs, and languages, and that its binding, relay, and gaze heads appear at every model size from 2B to 32B. This work allows us to investigate how a VLM turns a question and an image into a sequence of answers, layer by layer and token by token. More broadly, it opens a way to study how models plan over complex multi-step tasks with long rollouts. Our project is available at https://plan.baulab.info/
authors: Rohit Gandikota, Arnab Sen Sharma, Adam Belfki

title: Beyond Job Titles: Interpreting Early-Career Job Advertisements with Sparse Autoencoders and Semantic Clustering
abstract: Job titles and job descriptions alone provide limited insight into how technical roles differ in a changing job market. To assess how such roles differ in their work and industry applications, we design and compare two methods based on deep learning and transformer representations using 36,081 early-career job postings collected from LinkedIn in the United States between December 2025 and October 2026. We first apply PERC, short for Preprocessing (P), Embedding (E), Dimensionality Reduction (R) and Clustering (C). We employ GPT-6 Luna to classify job description passages into Team context, Role task and Qualifications. We then create combinations of these sections and examine whether embedding and clustering the segmented passages produce meaningful semantic clusters about different job roles. We use Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) to rank observed differences between embedding distributions and employ a pretrained sparse autoencoder (SAE) to extract features from layer-19 representations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Lastly, we employ GPT-6 Luna to come up with hypotheses about job roles' feature patterns, and GPT-6.1 Terra to investigate whether those patterns exist in held-out job descriptions from unseen companies. Some example findings include Data Scientist advertisements placing more emphasis on machine learning model development, Data Analyst advertisements on reporting business performance, and Machine Learning Engineer advertisements on applying developed models in real-world settings. We also observe differences in the applications described by Data Analyst and Business Analyst advertisements across selected months, although our dataset's scale and uneven coverage limit their interpretation. Overall, we present a realistic application of SAEs and PERC to unstructured textual data and examine how automated insight extraction could support manual analysis of job descriptions.
authors: Yisong Cao, Leah Kim, Brian Wright

title: Reading or Remembering? Measuring Temporal Contamination in Language Models
abstract: Language models are now used to read central-bank text for economic forecasting, but most were trained on text written after the documents they read. A model reading a 2021 FOMC statement may already know that inflation rose in 2022, so part of its apparent skill can be memory of the outcome, a temporal form of test-set contamination. We measure this memory on FOMC statements and minutes from 2000 to 2026 by comparing modern open models with chronologically consistent models, which are trained only on text from before a fixed date. Asked about past GDP outcomes given only a date, models that cannot know the answer still reach an AUC of up to 0.64 from priors on dates and eras, so chance is the wrong baseline. Against these memory-free models on the same questions, most modern models recall which years had strong growth. Membership-inference scores sort documents by era and document type rather than by whether a model saw them, as exact counts in an open pretraining corpus show. In real-time nowcasts, every lookahead premium we estimate on US GDP is smaller than the forecast comparison can detect at macroeconomic sample sizes, and none on GDP or inflation survives correction for multiple testing. Lookahead audits should therefore measure memory directly against memory-free models on the same items.
authors: Arunkumar V, Gangadharan G. R., S. Senthilkumar

title: Right Reason, Wrong Advice: Evaluating Recourse in LLM Explanations of Denied Requests
abstract: Language models increasingly write the explanations people receive when a rule system denies their request. If several rules deny the request independently, an explanation can name a true reason and still leave the person denied after they fix it. We call the missing property recourse validity: changing what the explanation cites, without changing what was asked for, can flip the decision. We compute it exactly, and a hitting-set argument predicts from the policy alone when a correct reason fails. In six of seven rule systems ported from access control and US benefit eligibility, a single correct reason almost never gives recourse when several reasons apply. Across 20 LLMs, checks of whether the cited reasons are correct, computed or asked of an LLM judge, are close to chance at spotting this failure, as the argument predicts. A strong judge asked whether acting on the explanation would work does spot it. Stronger and reasoning models do better but still fail on many denials with four or more independent reasons. Asking for every rule helps every open model with room to improve. Explanations of eligibility decisions should be built from the decision function and judged by whether acting on them works.
authors: Arunkumar V

title: Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the match can be decoded from their hidden states. We trace where this information is lost in Qwen3-VL-2B/4B/8B/32B, InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B on synthetic shape matching, HPatches point correspondence, and SPair-71k semantic correspondence, comparing input-matched probes with calibrated outputs. The models fail at two distinct points. Exact copies are compared and the result reaches the answer position, but the output does not use it, whether or not the shapes have names. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but are only weakly compared and never reach the answer position. The comparison runs through 16 to 32 attention heads that let tokens of the second image attend to the first. Redistributing their attention at fixed mass removes up to 32 points of accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads, and their attention is gated by salience and weighted by content. Training only these heads (0.02% of the parameters) recovers 25 to 28 points on SPair-71k and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. Unconstrained LoRA adapters, which reach higher accuracy, converge on the same heads: inserting only these heads' attention into the base model recovers 21-51% of an adapter's gain, mostly through changed inputs to the heads. Across all 14 trained arms, the selectivity of this small head set tracks the accuracy they reach, and it is read directly from attention, without probes or retraining. The gain in selectivity is not a by-product of more attention to the first image: it comes mostly from the wrong options no longer being drawn to the marked reference.
authors: Zhaoning Zhang

title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle
abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.
authors: Arunkumar V, Manoranjan Gandhudi, Gangadharan G. R.

title: Evaluating Cultural Reasoning and Robustness in LLMs for Spanish Political Discourse
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to interpret, generate, and mediate public-facing language, which makes their reliability especially consequential in politically sensitive settings. Although sentiment analysis is a common task in this area, affective meaning in social media discourse is often conveyed through culturally situated and pragmatically indirect cues that are not well captured by label-centric evaluation alone. In this paper, we evaluate the robustness of LLMs for sentiment analysis of Spanish political discourse from social media, with emphasis on culturally situated affective interpretation. We introduce a diagnostic protocol that combines three independent human annotation views into Gold and Ambiguous subsets, and extends the corpus with a Synthetic subset built from sentiment-flipped counterfactuals selected through model-conditioned perplexity and LLM-as-a-judge criteria. Using this framework, we compare proprietary and open-weight models under zero-shot and few-shot prompting, focusing on predictive robustness across human agreement conditions and counterfactual shift. Our results show that annotation ambiguity and counterfactual perturbation reveal failure modes that conventional evaluation on the original corpus tends to obscure. GPT-4.1-mini remains the most stable among the evaluated models, whereas the two smaller open-weight models degrade more markedly under synthetic perturbations, and few-shot prompting provides only limited gains. Overall, the paper contributes a reproducible protocol for robustness-oriented evaluation in political sentiment analysis, an empirical characterization of model behavior under ambiguity and sentiment-flipped counterfactuals, and a publicly available Spanish social media dataset with three-way human sentiment annotations.
authors: Jorge Valverde-Rebaza, Nathan Garcia-Larios, Karime Ruvalcaba-Perez

title: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier
abstract: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. For an executable policy over an enumerable context space this minimal sufficient reason can be computed exactly, so an explanation is scored against ground truth rather than a proxy for it. We use that exactness to ask what a model can learn from a verifier that has no error in it. The explainer sees one request and one decision, never the policy, and has thirty turns in which it may call the policy on altered requests and ask whether a candidate set of facts is sufficient. Frontier models find the exact reason about half the time with the tools alone, and one sentence telling them to shrink the answer lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%. A 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 traces of the deletion algorithm reaches 92% on the policy it was trained on. Teacher kind is what moves this: at matched data size the algorithm-taught student leads the frontier-taught one in all three training seeds, and the two arms never overlap. What the student learns is a fixed schedule of sufficiency checks, and the schedule does not travel. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. The oracle made the effect of training legible, but it did not make training better.
authors: Arunkumar V, Manoranjan Gandhudi, Gangadharan G. R.

title: Embedding Cosine Measures Text Length Before It Measures Homogenization
abstract: Mean pairwise cosine similarity between transformer embeddings is a standard measure of whether online discourse is converging under generative AI. When the embeddings are mean-pooled outputs of an encoder never trained for sentence similarity, this measure mostly tracks text length. In 6.06 million Reddit comments, an uncentered DeBERTa-v3 measure had suggested that only conservative discourse broke toward homogeneity after late 2022. Truncating the same comments from 10 to 150 words raises their mean cosine by eight times the reported break. A placebo that swaps every comment for a random one of equal length reproduces 81% of the asymmetry, and a fixed-content simulation reproduces 78%. The leading principal direction carries 99.9% of raw DeBERTa homogeneity, and once length is handled the asymmetry disappears under every encoder. On 575,000 Stack Exchange answers the measure reports a post-ChatGPT homogenization of technical sites that the placebo fully reproduces, although answers grew longer. A census of 31 studies locates the risk where anisotropic encoders meet time-series or length-unequal designs. A reverse control on a well-known experiment shows that centering with renormalization can reverse a genuine effect. We propose a low-cost diagnostic protocol. Corrected measures show that the two political camps converged between 2019 and 2022 and stopped converging before ChatGPT. Cross-camp replies engage their targets more closely than same-camp replies.
authors: Fengming Liu, Mingyu Shu

title: Detection-Efficient Watermarking for Vision--Language Agents via Risk-Constrained Strength Allocation
abstract: Vision--language agents generate descriptions, decisions, and instructions that may be reused by users, downstream agents, and automated workflows, creating a need for provenance mechanisms that support content authenticity and post-deployment auditing without unnecessarily degrading response quality. We present a risk-aware semantic watermarking framework that combines predictive uncertainty with a zero-shot multimodal relevance-risk proxy to allocate watermark strength during decoding. A single risk penalty $λ$ exposes a continuous operating frontier, allowing deployment-time selection of a detection--quality trade-off without model retraining. At a selected operating point, mean watermark strength is reduced by approximately 59.4\% relative to fixed-strength watermarking, while perplexity change falls from 0.3634 to 0.1689 and clean/paraphrased ROC-AUC reaches 0.9552/0.9459. A matched-strength analysis shows that this advantage reflects the allocation policy rather than lower average intervention: at comparable mean strength, risk-constrained allocation achieves substantially higher ROC-AUC than fixed, entropy-only, and criticality-only policies, identifying it as detection-efficient rather than quality-dominant. We further show that threshold calibration on finite samples produces substantial false-positive-rate drift, motivating calibration variance reporting as standard practice for auditable provenance.
authors: Dumindu Samaraweera, Prashant Shekhar

title: Jetriever: Shifting Agent Memory Retrieval from Similarity to Utility
abstract: Whether a stored memory helps answer a user's question often depends on world knowledge rather than surface similarity. Jetriever replaces similarity search with full-pool utility scoring: given a query, it uses Jev, an LLM-derived System One decision model, to score every stored memory for the probability that it is useful to the answer, ranking the memory pool directly by those probabilities. On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, Jetriever places the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases (versus 1.6% for BM25 and 0.0% for MiniLM with user-turn indexing) and reaches 76.0% end-to-end Application, compared with at most 16.0% across published retrieval and memory systems. A controlled 20-question comparison disentangles recognizing implicit evidence from ranking it properly: Jev and Qwen3.5-9B both recover 90% of gold exchanges within the top 50 (versus 30% for the BERT-based decision model Laya), yet at rank 1 Jev reaches 85% while Qwen3.5-9B drops to 40%. On a dimension-proportional random sample of 60 MemoryAgentBench questions, Jetriever raises the four-dimension average from 44.3% (ReFind) to 55.4%, at a mean retrieval cost of USD 0.00834 per InMind query and USD 0.03103 per MAB query. Together, these results show that effective utility retrieval hinges on combining broad world knowledge, calibrated ranking probabilities, and affordable full-pool evaluation.
authors: Ruizhe Li, Licheng Zhang, Mingxuan Du

title: Balanced Twin Weight Factorization for Efficient MLLMs
abstract: Weight Factorization (WF) methods aim to reduce a model's latency, memory, or both. These typically decompose a pretrained model into two or more factors that approximate the original model weights with fewer parameters and floating point operations (FLOPs). However, translating fewer FLOPs into reduced latency is challenging for WF methods in practice due to overhead introduced by replacing a single large weight matrix with multiple smaller ones. To address this, we propose Balanced Twin Weight Factorization (BTWF), which uses the unique structure of factorized models to simultaneously lower latency and increase learning capacity. Specifically, BTWF operates in the shared basis WF setting, where two or more layers are decomposed into a shared basis matrix and a layer-specific mixing matrix. If these shared layers have the same input (i.e., are twins), then we need only perform this shared forward pass once, reducing inference time. However, twin layers are often of varying sizes, and methods from prior work tend to favor the larger layer. In contrast, our approach boosts performance by combining Factor Component Balancing (FCB), which ensures every shared member is well represented in the selected factors, with Block Contribution Balancing (BCB), which considers downstream model effects. Further, we also show that an overparameterized BTWF, where some layer's factors result in higher FLOPs than the original during training, can boost task performance without additional resources at test time. Experiments on six models over nine benchmarks show BTWF obtains a 2-6% gain over the state-of-the-art without expensive finetuning (1-3.5% gain with it) at comparable computational costs.
authors: Bryan A. Plummer, Shan Lu, Keval Doshi

title: A Scalable Multi Task Learning Framework for Modeling Demographic Disagreements in Annotation Tasks
abstract: Annotators from different demographic backgrounds often disagree in systematic ways due to varying lived experiences, cultural contexts, and their relationship to the content. When such disagreement occurs, one group's perspective may sometimes warrant prioritization because they hold an epistemically advantaged standpoint or bear greater stake in the outcome. For example, when assessing toxicity of posts on social media, it may be important to prioritize a targeted group's viewpoint. We propose a Stakeholder-Aware Joint Multi-Task Learning (SAJ-MTL) framework to jointly model demographic disagreement both across- and within- annotator groups. The model uses conditional gradient routing to handle sparsity induced by group-conditional labeling, and parameterization supports customized weighting of groups in different task settings. SAJ-MTL improves group-level performance in toxicity detection through better context-aware understanding of demographic-sensitive content. Only annotator group-membership information is required, which is more practical than existing methods requiring more privacy-invasive individual-level annotator details. Our scalable architecture is also computationally efficient to support large-scale deployment.
authors: Soumyajit Gupta, Maria De-Arteaga, Matthew Lease

title: Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers
abstract: Researchers at MIT recently reported that GPT-6 Astra, a frontier large language model (LLM), can write the weights of small neural networks directly in a single reply, and can read the raw weights of small networks to say what they were trained to do. In a three-day sprint, we replicated and extended these results. Our four findings: (1) Writing weights reproduces. Astra's networks for the game Breakout scored 514, 550 and 307 (versus MIT's 517), and scored just as well on two modified versions of Breakout. Claude Opus 5.5 can also write working networks, but often runs out of output tokens. (2) What is new is translating programs into weights. Earlier models could write a good policy as code a generation before they could write network weights, and the networks the models write behave like compiled programs: two models independently decompiled Astra's Breakout network into Python matching its actions in all tested states. On classifying handwritten digits, Astra's networks scored 50% on average, below a simple classifier (82%). (3) Reading weights is mostly reading the input layer. Astra and Opus 5.5 identify which game a network plays almost perfectly, but on three new games we designed and trained ourselves, Astra recovered where things are on the board, while mostly missing how the game works. (4) Auditing from weights alone is possible but shallow. Without executing code, Astra picked out a small language model poisoned during training in 10 of 10 runs, one poisoned by extra training afterwards in 7 of 10, and a malicious adapter in 23 of 32 cases, but never identified the trigger or malicious behaviour. Open-weight models lag behind. From this early study, we conclude that LLMs can read and write small networks, but that this currently amounts to compiling hand-designed programs and reading the layout of the input layer. It is a promising but early tool for interpretability.
authors: Roksana Goworek, Alexander Hickey, Federico Nanni

title: Just sort it! A note on the LP behind rank-one anti-loop edits
abstract: Weight-space programming removes the thinking loops of a small reasoning model by a rank-one edit W' = W + u v^T of an MLP output matrix, where u is a loop direction and v is the solution of a sparse Linear Program (LP) over the neuron activations. We investigate whether the LP is needed. We replace it by a sort: we take the 8 neurons whose activation has the smallest coefficient of variation, and give them equal shares of the push that the LP solution realizes. On Qwen3.5-0.8B the sorted edit scores 67.0% on 1000 problems (MATH-500 and GSM8K) against 67.4% for the LP edit and 9.5% for the unedited model; the paired difference is -0.4 points, with 95% confidence interval [-2.9, +2.1], inside a non-inferiority margin of 5 points declared before the runs. On three further sampling seeds the difference is -0.6 points, interval [-2.0, +0.8], and -0.8 points, interval [-2.3, +0.6], when the dose is set without the LP. The sort does not solve the LP, but the neurons it shares with the LP solution carry most of its mean push. The outcome is that, on this model, the edit acts as a nearly constant bias along u.
authors: Matteo Fischetti

title: Rubric-Based AES with LLM Ensembles: Scoring of Student Responses in Critical Online Reasoning Using Ensembles of LLMs
abstract: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.
authors: Daniel Baumartz, Alexander Mehler, Patrick Schrottenbacher

title: AuXSpec: Learning to Autoformalize Program Specifications via Executable Postconditions
abstract: Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended behavior.
