title: Topological analysis of permeability tensor in anisotropic porous media
abstract: The permeability of an anisotropic porous medium is a tensor whose off-diagonal components, which describe the deflection of the macroscopic flux away from the driving force, are small and change sign under reflections. We ask whether direction-aware topological data analysis can predict the full permeability tensor of three-dimensional porous media directly from their geometry. We introduce two direction-aware topological descriptors for flow problems: a cone-based filtration, adapted from our earlier work on the elastic stiffness tensor, and a throat-scale filtration built on the distance transform of the pore space. Using permeability tensors computed with the lattice Boltzmann method, we compare them with a comprehensive set of non-topological baselines, comprising statistical microstructure descriptors and physics-based permeability estimators. The topological descriptors are most informative for the off-diagonal components, which the baselines capture least well. There the throat-scale filtration alone outperforms every non-topological descriptor set, including the union of all statistical descriptors and physics-based estimators, and adding it to the baselines consistently improves the prediction. We also confirm the approach on real rock data.
authors: Rafał Topolnicki, Paweł Dłotko, Maciej Matyka

title: Reasoning Beyond Imitation: Observation Conditioned Distillation for Video LLMs
abstract: Reasoning distillation offers a promising approach to transfer temporal reasoning capabilities of powerful Video-LLMs to open-source student models. However, teacher and student Video-LLMs may construct different temporal observations from the same video due to the adoption of distinct video sampling pipelines. A reasoning trajectory valid under the teacher's observations may rely on evidence inaccessible to the student and thus cannot be directly executed based on the student's observations. We formalize this as a conditional target mismatch, thereby revealing the Reasoning Acquisition-Execution Gap. To bridge this gap, we propose an acquisition-to-execution framework that first distills teacher trajectories into a student reasoning prior and then further optimizes the execution capability of this prior across multiple observations. We further introduce Execution-Aware Reference Regularization, which retains the existing prior when it is executable under current observations, while allowing a greater degree of adaptive adjustment when it is not. Experiments across multiple Video-LLM backbones and six video reasoning benchmarks show that explicitly optimizing observation-conditioned execution consistently outperforms supervised distillation and standard RL-based optimization, with gains extending to held-out out-of-domain benchmarks.
authors: Junzhou Chen, Jindong Wang, Gang Zhou

title: Continuous-Time LQR from a Single Discrete-Time Off-Policy Batch
abstract: We study discounted continuous-time linear--quadratic regulation (LQR) with unknown drift parameters and additive noise, using a single batch of discrete-time off-policy transitions. Discrete-time methods target a policy tied to the training interval, while shortening this interval can make learning from finite data more sensitive to noise. Learning an accurate continuous-time controller therefore requires balancing discretization and finite-sample errors while preserving stability throughout policy improvement. We develop a drift-only policy iteration algorithm, termed PhiBE-PI, using one quadratic state--action critic for policy evaluation and explicit greedy improvement. Reusing the batch makes later policies depend on the data. Exploiting the quadratic structure of LQR, we show that the data enter every policy evaluation only through one policy-independent empirical matrix, so a single high-probability bound controls all iterates. For sufficiently large discount~$β$, small observation intervals, and a sufficiently large batch, we prove that all iterates are stabilizing for the discounted problem and converge quadratically to a data-dependent fixed point. The gain bound separates iteration, finite-sample, and discretization errors. In this regime, the finite-sample and discretization terms scale as $1/(β\sqrt{nΔt})$ and $Δt/β$, respectively. The bounds thus reveal a tradeoff: at a fixed batch size, finer observations reduce discretization error but increase finite-sample error. Because PhiBE-PI approximates the continuous-time optimal gain rather than a discrete-time one, its policy can remain near-optimal when deployed at faster control rates. Experiments confirm this advantage over discrete-time Bellman-equation baselines when the observation interval is small relative to the system's time scale.
authors: Chaorui Yao, Yuhua Zhu

title: LAF-ECG: Multi-Resolution Lead-Aware Fusion of Time-Series and Language Foundation Models for ECG Classification
abstract: Automated electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation has advanced substantially with deep learning, yet many methods remain task-specific and label-dependent. Large language models (LLMs) and time-series foundation models (TSFMs) offer complementary pretrained representations, but integrating them is challenging because of mismatched feature spaces and the lead- and scale-dependent structure of ECG signals. We propose LAF-ECG (Lead-Aware Foundation Fusion for ECG), a dual-foundation framework that extends MedTsLLM with a lead-aware interface to a frozen TSFM backbone while retaining its reprogramming pathway. The proposed framework captures multi-resolution temporal context, fuses temporal and language-aligned ECG representations through adaptive residual integration, and employs branch-specific supervision with cross-branch alignment. LAF-ECG achieves 71.10% accuracy and 62.43% macro-F1 on PTB-XL, and 89.73% accuracy and 65.94% macro-F1 on Chapman-Shaoxing, outperforming MedTsLLM on both datasets. These results highlight the value of preserving lead-specific temporal structure when combining temporal and language foundation representations for ECG classification. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/kkianamm/LAF-ECG.
authors: Kiana Taktehrani, Maryam Hosseini, Amir Keynia

title: Randomized Weighted Distance Nearest Neighbor Classification
abstract: The nearest neighbor classifier is known to be memory-inefficient, and a popular solution is to compress its training data. Recently, a compression algorithm based on weighted distance nearest neighbor (WNN) was proposed, which has elegant theoretical properties and effective classification performance. However, its compression process is computationally expensive, for it performs a greedy search of the densest homogeneous balls in data space. In this paper, we propose a randomized variant RWNN. It simply randomizes the ball search process, and results in substantially reduced compression time (often 0.1%--1% of WNN's) and similar classification accuracy. RWNN also inherits several theoretical properties of WNN including consistency and a generalization bound. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate its efficacy.
authors: Shayan Shafaei, Naeem Shahabi Sani, Chao Lan

title: From States to Dynamics: Detecting Rule Violations in OthelloGPT
abstract: Sequence models trained on game moves have been shown to encode world models, with structured linear probes revealing the underlying game states. World models, however, are inherently dynamic: in deterministic board games, a set of rules constrain how states evolve over time. We therefore ask if and how OthelloGPT, a transformer trained only on Othello move sequences, manifests the rules of the game in its activation space. We divide the rules of Othello, and symmetrically their violations, into three classes: placing a disc on an empty square (R1), flanking an opponent's disc (R2), and moving in turn (R3). We find that linear probes accurately separate legal from illegal moves, and also distinguish between the three kinds of rule violations. We introduce an unsupervised rule-violation detector based on the step length of activations between consecutive moves, which identifies illegal moves above chance. We further improve our detection metric by computing step length in the latent space of select sparse autoencoders. Together, we find that OthelloGPT follows game rules of Othello to a large extent, and that we can detect rule violations using structured detectors on model activations.
authors: David L. Cao, Sai Sumedh R. Hindupur, Demba Ba

title: Learning-Augmented QUBO for Time-Expanded Multi-Commodity Flow
abstract: We study energy-aware multi-commodity flow on time-expanded graphs, a problem that captures dynamic routing in layered networks and is NP-hard in general. We formulate the problem as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization problem, give an explicit penalty coefficient that provably guarantees feasibility, and show that it is smaller than the standard bound by a factor of roughly the number of active links. The layered structure of the time-expanded graph yields three structural results: a treewidth bound that gives a fixed-parameter tractable exact algorithm in the bag size, a matrix-product-operator representation of small bond dimension, and a proof that the annealing gap of the associated Ising Hamiltonian is strictly positive for every instance with a unique optimum, uniformly over bounded windows. For learning-augmented routing, we bound the Hamming distance between a predicted and an optimal flow by the flow error, and prove a consistency guarantee: a hybrid algorithm that keeps the better of the prediction and the solver output returns a flow whose cost exceeds the optimum by a factor that grows linearly with the prediction error. The results are exact statements about the QUBO and its associated Ising Hamiltonian, and they hold for any physical implementation.
authors: Aikaterini Nikolidaki

title: Towards Global Counterfactual-Based Self-Explainable Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph Counterfactual Explanations (GCEs) have emerged as an effective approach for interpreting Graph Neural Network (GNN) predictions by identifying minimal graph modifications needed to change predictions. However, existing methods suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) They rely on a post-hoc explanation paradigm, where a separate explainer is trained after the GNN. This sequential optimization prevents the explainer from leveraging how the GNN learned its representations, often resulting in lower-quality explanations. (2) They are largely local, generating counterfactual explanations only for individual samples. Consequently, they fail to capture generalizable patterns across the data distribution, a crucial gap for applications like drug discovery, where global principles enable systematic decision-making across thousands of cases. To address these limitations, we propose GCSGNN (Global Counterfactual-based Self-explainable GNN), a unified framework that integrates counterfactual generation into the GNN architecture, encouraging explanations that faithfully reflect the model's decision-making process. Beyond local explanations, GCSGNN discovers shared latent patterns influencing predictions across graphs, yielding global (i.e., model-level) counterfactual explanations. We further introduce an efficient latent-space counterfactual mechanism that avoids the combinatorial complexity of discrete graph manipulation, enabling scalable discovery of generalizable modification patterns. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GCSGNN outperforms existing methods in generating effective counterfactual explanations. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/gcsgnn.
authors: Wendy Zheng, Yinhan He, Jundong Li

title: CrysLDM: Latent Diffusion Model for Crystal Material Generation
abstract: Generating new crystal materials with desirable chemical properties has long been a challenging task. Existing diffusion models operate in feature space, requiring complex diffusion architectures to model the joint distribution of atom types, coordinates, and lattice structures. This complexity increases the number of diffusion steps, leading to higher training and sampling costs. In this work, we aim to generate novel crystal materials within a time- and resource-constrained setup, where existing models are not well-suited. To address this, we propose CrysLDM, a novel latent diffusion model for 3D crystal materials, which integrates a variational autoencoder and a diffusion model. The VAE encoder maps 3D crystal structures into a latent space, where the diffusion model operates. Since CrysLDM leverages a smooth, lower-dimensional latent space, it simplifies the generative process and accelerates both training and inference. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets and tasks, we show that CrysLDM generates stable and valid materials with quality comparable to state-of-the-art methods, while being significantly more efficient in terms of computational resources and time.
authors: Subhojyoti Khastagir, Kishalay Das, Pawan Goyal

title: Exact on Paper: Which LLM Serving Shortcuts Flip Graded Answers, Measured Against the Noise of Reordering the Same Requests
abstract: Teams enable serving features such as prefix caching, chunked prefill and speculative decoding after checking that benchmark accuracy is unchanged, because the engine documents them as exact. Accuracy is an aggregate, so a feature can hold it while flipping which requests are answered correctly. We serve one 4B instruction model in vLLM under nine single feature configurations and five replicas of a reference configuration, grade 3,380 requests from five benchmarks in every run, and compare each candidate with a restart floor (fresh process) and a scheduling floor (same requests in a different order). With default kernels every configuration keeps accuracy within one point, and the seven exact features flip the graded outcome of 1.47% (95% CI 1.13 to 1.85) to 1.78% (1.39 to 2.20) of requests, none above the scheduling floor of 1.72%, while the FP8 KV cache flips 3.36% (2.80 to 3.96), as many as FP8 weights. With batch invariant kernels all seven exact features, speculative decoding included, reproduce the reference text on every request, while the FP8 KV cache still flips 3.91% (3.28 to 4.53) of graded outcomes. A gate that compares against a single replica pair rejected an unchanged configuration, so we recommend certifying a serving change under batch invariant kernels, where the floor is zero, or against a scheduling floor measured from at least three replicas.
authors: Sharven Rane

title: One Checkpoint, Four Converters: Per Input Disagreement After On Device Conversion and a Probe Set That Catches It
abstract: A model converted for on device or accelerated inference ships once its top 1 accuracy matches the source model. Accuracy can match while individual decisions change, and the converter, its INT8 recipe and its calibration draw each move them. We convert 5 public checkpoints (four ImageNet classifiers and a sentiment model) with the documented FP32 and INT8 recipes of ExecuTorch, LiteRT, ONNX Runtime and TensorRT and compare every top 1 decision with the PyTorch source on 7,854 images and 1,938 sentences. All 34 strict FP32 conversions reproduce every decision, yet each of the 4 vision INT8 recipes that keeps accuracy equivalent flips more than 1% of decisions: ONNX Runtime static INT8 flips 4.07% (95% CI [3.65, 4.53]) of ResNet 50 decisions while accuracy moves by -0.15 points, and two builds of that recipe from different calibration draws disagree on 3.44% [3.06, 3.88]. Where accuracy is kept, the flipped inputs are the ones the source model barely decides (AUROC of the source margin 0.90 to 0.97 on ResNet 50, every 95% CI inside [0.89, 0.98]), but our preregistered claim that this holds for every recipe fails on the two mobile networks, where INT8 breaks accuracy outright. A probe set of the 200 training inputs with the smallest source margin, chosen before any conversion, flags all 40 vision stacks (recall 95% CI [0.91, 1.00]) and all 6 text stacks that flip at least 0.5% of decisions and none of the exact FP32 conversions, so conversion checks should compare decisions on such a probe set, not accuracy.
authors: Sharven Rane

title: How Seasonal Reference Choice Changes the Apparent Gains of Chronos Models in Electricity Load Forecasting
abstract: When a forecasting model is said to beat a simple baseline, the size of that win depends on which baseline was used. We measure how much this matters for two zero-shot foundation models, Chronos-Bolt and Chronos-2, on hourly electricity load. The study uses 60 fixed cases drawn from eight series in four public collections, with forecasts 24 and 168 hours ahead and up to 2,048 hours of history. Each model is compared with daily persistence, weekly persistence, a weekday hybrid, a daily-weekly blend, and a reference chosen from these on a validation period. We keep every origin-level forecast and estimate uncertainty with paired circular block bootstrap intervals using 168- and 336-hour blocks. A week ahead, Bolt clearly beats weekly persistence in 21 of 30 cases but the validation-selected reference in only 14, and its median gain falls from 17.3% to 11.9%. For Chronos-2 the clear-win counts are 18 and 15. Chronos-2 has lower week-ahead MAE than Bolt in 24 cases, yet only 12 of those differences are clear. The selected reference is not always the harder baseline, since on some test windows it does worse than weekly persistence. The choice of baseline therefore changes both how large the reported gain is and how sure we can be of it. The results are exploratory: the series and windows are related, an earlier pilot was inspected, pretraining overlap cannot be ruled out, and the case-level intervals are not corrected for multiple comparisons.
authors: ChandraMohan K

title: JKO-GRPO: Augmenting GRPO with Wasserstein Proximal Steps for Flow-Matching VLAs
abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_0,π_{0.5}$ generate continuous action chunks by flow matching, and online reinforcement learning (RL) can improve them beyond supervised fine-tuning. Existing methods, such as Flow-GRPO and $π_{\mathrm{RL}}$, optimize likelihood ratios of stochastic denoising transitions, which reweight the sampled actions by their advantages but do not use the distances between them. We propose JKO-GRPO, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, with two contributions: (1) At each state, we treat the group of sampled actions as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) step. We use a soft discrete $c$-transform to construct transport targets from group-relative advantages and combine shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler onto these targets and combined with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective without Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. (2) We extend this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching: we select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.
authors: Jiyong Kwon, Yikun Bai, Amirhossein Mollaali

title: Attacking Tabular Foundation Models: An Experimental Taxonomy of Context Poisoning and Test-Time Evasion
abstract: Tabular foundation models condition predictions on labeled examples supplied at inference time, creating an attack surface that differs from conventional model training. We study four manipulation families (label flipping, backdoor context poisoning, clean-label context selection, and test-time evasion) and organize them by attack stage, label consistency, and distributional realism. TabPFN-2.5, TabICL, and XGBoost are evaluated on CIC-IDS2017 and N-BaIoT using a common preprocessing and evaluation pipeline. Backdoor context poisoning provides strong targeted control over the in-context models with little change in clean accuracy, whereas selecting real, correctly labeled boundary-crowding rows causes no systematic accuracy degradation up to a 20% bias fraction. A simplified surrogate-transfer constrained PGD attack inspired by, but not equivalent to, CAPGD also produces test-time evasion, outperforming equal-budget random noise in most settings. The comparison shows that attack effectiveness depends strongly on both where manipulation occurs and how much freedom the attacker has to alter the data.
authors: Ramak Nassiri, Sujan Kumar Reddy Challa, Feroz Ahmed

title: Aggregation Dispersion: An Information-Geometric Diagnostic of Oversmoothing in Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) learn node representations by iteratively aggregating information from neighbors, but stacking too many layers causes all representations to converge, an effect known as oversmoothing. We propose a geometric perspective on this phenomenon. At each depth $k$, the propagation operator assigns to every node $v$ a walk distribution $p_v^{(k)}$, a probability distribution over source nodes. These walk distributions form a point cloud on the probability simplex, whose contraction to a single point characterizes complete mixing of the propagation operator, and thus oversmoothing. To measure this contraction, we use the Fisher-Rao metric, the unique Riemannian metric on the simplex invariant up to scale under sufficient statistics, whose scaled chordal distance under the square-root embedding $p \mapsto \sqrt{p}$ is the Hellinger distance. The resulting diagnostic, the aggregation dispersion $D_k$, is the variance of the embedded point cloud on the unit sphere. We prove that: (i) $D_k = 0$ if and only if the $k$-th step propagation matrix has rank one, a necessary and sufficient condition for complete operator mixing; (ii) $D_k$ is non-increasing with depth; (iii) the spectral gap of the propagation matrix controls the rate of this decay; and (iv) for contractive MPNNs, the aggregation dispersion upper-bounds the representation dispersion up to graph- and initialization-dependent constants. Across 14 model configurations and 11 datasets, $D_k$ attains the highest mean absolute Pearson correlation with test accuracy across depths among eight diagnostics ($|r| = 0.721$, using log-transformed diagnostic values), numerically comparable to the post-training effective rank ($|r| = 0.688$), while requiring no training.
authors: Abdessalam Ed-dib, Amine Mohamed Aboussalah

title: Reset Dependence Is Embodied: Training Protocol Changes Which Morphologies Appear Optimal
abstract: Robot co-design benchmarks rank bodies after training their controllers under a fixed episode protocol, but that protocol can change the ranking itself. Consequently, two studies can select different bodies from the same corpus even when they use the same task and evaluator. We study one part of that protocol, the reset rule, which ends a training episode when the robot's torso falls below a height threshold. We train proximal policy optimization (PPO) controllers for 100 DERL-evolved UNIMAL bodies with this threshold at 20% of each body's starting torso height (Standard), at 50% (Strict), or with no threshold (Reset-free), and score every controller with the same evaluator. The threshold changes which bodies look best: the rankings after Strict and Reset-free training correlate at only 0.21, against about 0.89 if seed noise were the only difference. Removing fall resets costs some bodies far more than others. Bodies evolved on flat ground lose 45% of their per-step reward relative to Standard training, and those evolved on variable terrain only 16%. Permutation tests over bodies support this difference, and on 24 bodies, flat-ground bodies gain the most from Strict over Reset-free training under both PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC). Choosing bodies by their worst reward across the three protocols costs little: in sample, they keep at least 91% of the reward of each protocol's best bodies, and over 80% averaged across held-out seeds. Co-design benchmarks should state their reset rule, test whether their rankings depend on it, and report bodies that stay strong across protocols. Project page: https://reset-dependence.github.io.
authors: Kevin Qiu, Zhao Yang, Marek Cygan

title: GeoFusion: An Uncertain Machine Learning Framework for Sensor Fusion
abstract: High positioning precision is a critical requirement in many Global Positioning System (GPS) applications, yet achieving it with affordable smartphone sensors remains an open challenge. Existing approaches treat each GPS observation as an absolute point, discarding the uncertainty inherent in the measurement conditions and leaving the cooperative potential of multiple phones observing the same location untapped. In this work, we propose GeoFusion, a three-stage uncertain machine learning framework for cooperative sensor fusion. In the first stage, each GPS observation is modeled as an uncertain object using one of two proposed models: the volcano function, grounded in satellite geometry, and the empirically derived mountain function, built from the statistical structure of real smartphone data. In the second stage, uncertain objects are clustered by location event using partitional and graph-based algorithms. In the third stage, the cluster output is refined using filter-based and learning-based estimators. Experiments on the Google Smartphone Decimeter Challenge dataset show that uncertainty modeling is a primary driver of precision gains: the mountain function significantly outperforms the geometry-only volcano function, and uncertainty-aware UK-medoids significantly outperforms its certain counterpart, k-medoids. A post-clustering deep neural network further refines the cluster estimates, and the recommended configuration achieves a mean absolute error of 2.90 +/- 0.15 meters on held-out test drives, comparable to and on average below the best reported single-phone precision of approximately 3 meters, demonstrating the potential of cooperative uncertainty-aware fusion for affordable GPS sensors.
authors: Basant Ahmed Mounir Abdelhamid, Amr T. Abdel-Hamid

title: CoHABIT: Complementary Evaluation of Furniture Layouts through Spatial Rules and Household Routines
abstract: We introduce CoHABIT, a framework for evaluating furniture layouts through complementary spatial rules and household routines. Static assessment captures geometric validity, ergonomic access, functional organization, and configurable design preferences, including Feng Shui. Dynamic assessment uses learned resident policies to simulate everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens in multi-agent households. Controlled comparisons show how spatial criteria and household behavior reveal distinct aspects of layout quality, while resident profiles and scheduling influence furnishing rankings. Independent verification of household needs grounds dynamic comparisons in observed outcomes, enabling interpretable assessments of how furnished environments serve different households.
authors: Ewsey Obzherin, Samira Atlangirieva, Anastasia Antsiferova

title: Vanishing Initialization Turns Diagonal Tensor Gradient Flow into Greedy Matching
abstract: We study gradient-flow (GF) learning of tensors from vanishing initialization in canonical polyadic (CP) factorization models. For tensors of order $ν\geq3$ whose targets are diagonal in mode-wise orthonormal bases, we prove that the limiting learning dynamics follows a simple greedy bipartite matching process. Each rank-one component of the model, called an atom, can potentially learn each rank-one component of the target, called a scalar sector. Every atom--sector pair has an initialization-dependent activation clock, representing the time at which the atom would grow to macroscopic size in that sector if the pair evolved in isolation. Processing these clocks in increasing order and selecting a pair whenever neither its atom nor its sector has been selected before determines the sequence of actual learning events. We prove that the GF trajectory converges to the corresponding staircase of learned target components. The task of learning modular addition by a CP model with complex weights falls exactly into this framework after Fourier diagonalization. Its activation clocks are independent and identically distributed, allowing us to combine the GF reduction with known random matching asymptotics and derive an explicit, distribution-free large-system loss curve after time reparametrization. We also obtain an asymptotic formula relating this curve to the original GF training time. For models with real weights, conjugate Fourier modes instead form two-dimensional blocks with richer internal structure. We characterize their rank and border-rank cascade and conjecture that the corresponding GF dynamics follows interleaved multi-stage learning processes.
authors: Dmitry Yarotsky, Eugene Golikov, Yaroslav Gusev

title: What Test-Time Training Corrects in Latent World Models? A Slow-Fast Approach
abstract: Latent world models plan toward a goal by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions, but under the distribution shift, prediction errors can lead the planner astray. Test-time training using executed actions helps, yet what it corrects and whether its updates should persist across episodes remains unclear. We address both by analyzing the world model's prediction error. On PushObj, an object-pushing task, we probe multiple actions from the same state and decompose the error into an offset shared across actions and an action-dependent component. The offset effectively shifts the planner's goal, and AdaJEPA mainly tracks it: the common shift alone recovers 91% of its planning gain. Part of the offset is episode-specific, so carrying its correction into the next episode does not help and may even hurt. The remaining offset recurs across episodes and action-dependent error can be or needs to be learned and retained from many episodes. Our sft-JEPA therefore uses two learners on different timescales: a fast learner that tracks the offset and resets each episode, and a slow LoRA learner that accumulates recurring knowledge across episodes. Across PushObj, PointMaze, zero-shot planning on RoboCasa (with DINO-WM), and OGBench (with LeWAM), sft-JEPA leads all benchmark averages, improving planning success over AdaJEPA by up to 22 points.
authors: Shuaicheng Niu, Guohao Chen, Kevin Z. Shen

title: A Closed-Form Soft Spectral Partition for Adaptive Mode Decomposition
abstract: Density-based Adaptive Mode Decomposition (DAMD) shows that the Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) objective, restricted to hard binary partitions, is equivalent to weighted K-means clustering, enabling automatic mode detection. The equivalence concerns detection only; extraction with hard Voronoi masks introduces boundary artefacts. This paper develops a soft extraction theory independent of the detector. First, the hard-partition equivalence is shown to be an algebraic identity that holds if and only if the weights are binary; hard and soft extraction are optima of two different functionals (linear K-means and regularised quadratic VMD) over the same simplex. Second, the regularised soft VMD problem is proved to have a closed-form global optimum, unique on the support of the spectrum: the Lorentzian-weighted partition $s_k^*(ω)\propto[1+2α(ω-ω_k)^2]^{-1}$. Every fixed point of the VMD ADMM mode update is proportional to $|ω-ω_k|^{-2}$; when the dual ascent enforces reconstruction, it is the $α\to\infty$ endpoint of this family. The Lorentzian shape at finite $α$ is therefore a consequence of the regulariser, and $α$ controls how closely the allocation approaches that fixed point. Third, under a Lorentzian spectral prior the partition equals the minimum mean-square error (MMSE) estimator of each mode in the low-noise limit, tying $α$ to the inverse squared mode bandwidth. Since the partition needs only detected centre frequencies, the extraction rule can be switched without recomputing detection. Synthetic experiments with known ground truth test the predictions; four categories of real signals show how much the two allocations differ.
authors: Hao Jia, Chunyu Yang, Fan Feng

title: RumiFold: Teaching an LLM to Natively Fold Proteins and Reason About Their Function
abstract: Can we teach a general-purpose language model to fold proteins? And if so, what does learning to fold enable beyond structure prediction itself? We introduce RumiFold, a pretrained chat model that learns to predict protein structures directly from its own hidden states. RumiFold processes proteins through repeated folding passes, then uses these folded representations to answer questions in natural language. It achieves folding accuracy comparable to dedicated single-representation models such as SimpleFold, alongside state-of-the-art performance on Gene Ontology protein function prediction and free-text function description. We find that folding pretraining organizes the model's hidden states around protein function, creating an internal per-residue workspace that is biologically grounded. Causal interventions show that this folded workspace links structure and language when RumiFold predicts function, providing rich representations for biomolecular reasoning. We see RumiFold as a step toward native biomolecular intelligence: where protein-based computations and language-based reasoning become integrated capabilities of general-purpose language models. Code, data, and models are available at: https://rumifold.baulab.info
authors: Kevin Lu, David Bau, Wengong Jin

title: Optimal Bandits with Switching Costs: $(T/\log(T))^{2/3}$ Regret
abstract: We study adversarial bandits with switching costs. For $K$ arms, $T$ rounds, unit switching costs, and oblivious losses in $[0,1]$, we prove that the minimax regret is \begin{equation*} Θ\!\left(\min\left\{T, \frac{K^{1/3}T^{2/3}}{\log^{2/3}(2+T/K)}\right\}\right)\,. \end{equation*} This shows that simple blocking, which plays one arm throughout each block, is suboptimal. Our algorithm makes at most a constant number of switches at random times within each block. The key idea for the improvement is to extract more information per switch by giving greater weight to observations near switching times. We also introduce detours, during which the learner temporarily plays a newly sampled arm. Larger observed losses make a detour more likely. These detours cancel temporal correlation terms induced by blocking while preserving the observations used in the estimates. A matching lower bound follows from a refined analysis of a modified multiscale random walk construction.
authors: Chenyu Gan

title: Phase-Conditioned Action Contracts for Auditable Microsurgical Control
abstract: Staged robotic procedures may reuse a fixed-dimensional policy output even though the admissible motions and physical meanings of its coordinates change across phases. We call this action-semantic shift. To address it, we propose a phase-conditioned executable policy that separates learned action proposal from deterministic command formation. Phase-specific heads generate proposals, while an action contract removes inadmissible components, enforces state-dependent bounds, and decodes the remaining action into phase-dependent task-space commands. We further introduce failure-focused local repair and a read-only provenance trace for exact command replay and rule-level auditing. Across three held-out retinal-injection evaluation blocks, our method achieves $94.27\pm0.64\%$ procedural completion and $64.40\pm2.43\%$ success within $35\,μ\mathrm{m}$, with no hard violations. Applying the contract and decoder to the same frozen Correction network raises completion from $12.27\%$ to $90.47\%$. The trace exactly reconstructs 96,350 commands, and all 1,996 binding interventions follow their declared effects. These results show the importance of explicit executable action semantics for auditable staged microsurgical control.
authors: Jiaxi You, Yiwei Shi, Yanlin Li

title: HKD-ACPA: Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation Adversarial Cyber-Physical Attacks in Power Grids
abstract: Learning-based algorithms assist power-grid control centers in localizing transmission-line attacks, yet existing adversarial attacks typically require white-box access or repeated online queries. We study a practical zero-query setting in which an adversary coordinates physical, denial-of-service (DoS), and false data injection (FDI) attacks using only local measurements and historical detector outputs. To bridge the input-view asymmetry between local adversarial observations and DoS-masked control-center measurements, we propose Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation Adversarial Cyber-Physical Attacks (HKD-ACPA). HKD-ACPA distills historical detector predictions into a heterogeneous graph surrogate ensemble and trains a residual calibration module to correct the view-induced logit discrepancy. Over this calibrated surrogate, we formulate sparse, magnitude-bounded FDI synthesis with a group-balanced objective that jointly induces missed detections and false alarms, and solve the resulting hybrid discrete--continuous problem via bi-level projected gradient-based proximal policy optimization (PGPPO). Experiments on the IEEE 30-bus and 118-bus systems show that HKD-ACPA outperforms all surrogate-based baselines across every sparsity budget and surpasses online-query attacks in eight of ten system--budget settings without querying the detector model.
authors: Junhao Ren, Honglin Gao, Shuo Feng

title: Optimal Labelling Designs for Sequential Decisions on Language Model Updates
abstract: When a large language model (LLM) is updated, its developer must decide whether accuracy improved, worsened or stayed within a tolerance. An LLM judge can assess every prompt cheaply but imperfectly, while human labels are costly. We propose Sequential Decisions with Optimal Labelling Designs (SOLD), which labels one prompt at a time, uses the judge to correct the estimate of the change in accuracy and to choose the prompts, and stops once the evidence is conclusive. A wrong decision has probability at most a prespecified level whenever labelling stops. The commonly used Neyman allocation minimises the variance of the estimate and therefore rarely labels prompts that the judge is confident about. It can need far more draws when the outcomes of these prompts could still fall far below the judge's prediction. We instead derive the design that gathers evidence fastest, which labels each prompt with probability at least proportional to how far its outcome could fall below the prediction. As the level tends to zero, no procedure based on the judge-corrected estimates needs fewer draws than SOLD. In simulations and on the EVOUNA and MMLU-Pro datasets, SOLD needed fewer labels than the other methods.
authors: Doudou Zhou, Jiahui Xie, Yue Liu

title: BenchMint: From Real-World Tasks to Executable Benchmarks
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) need evaluations of everyday reasoning and tool use, such as planning itineraries under user constraints and grounding numerical answers in evidence. We introduce BenchMint, an automated benchmark-construction workflow, and Daily-Life, its collection of 100 selected tasks across 11 real-world domains. BenchMint jointly constructs tasks and scoring criteria from the same source documents. Language-model judges assess possible answers against these criteria using tool traces and private evidence. We report 26 model/harness configurations, including GPT, Claude and Gemini families; 17 have complete domain profiles. These are descriptive configuration results, not a controlled model ranking. In one selected travel task, we corrected the reference total from 320 to 380 minutes while keeping both answers unchanged. The incorrect answer's arithmetic verdict switched from pass to fail; the correct answer's switched from fail to pass. With one ballot per cell, this exposes a reference error without establishing repeatability or collection-wide validity. Incomplete construction comparisons establish no general advantage of joint authoring or feedback-guided revision.
authors: Zining Huang, Zuo Wang, Mengyao Zhang

title: SleepXA: Composing Pretrained Neural and Cardiac Foundation Models for Sleep Representation Learning
abstract: Physiological signals recorded during sleep provide synchronized views of neural, cardiac, respiratory, and other bodily systems, while preserving modality-specific information. Existing EEG and ECG foundation models already capture rich but distinct physiological structure, motivating an alternative to training a multimodal sleep model from scratch: composing existing pretrained models. We introduce SleepXA, a framework that uses synchronized polysomnography (PSG) to compose independently pretrained neural and cardiac foundation models. SleepXA combines pretrained EEG and ECG encoders with lightweight encoders for additional PSG modalities, and learns shared and modality-specific representations through sleep-guided alignment. We pretrain SleepXA on 9,230 overnight PSG recordings from three large cohorts and evaluate it on 27 downstream tasks spanning sleep representation, clinical and disease prediction, and daytime physiological transfer. SleepXA ranks among the top two methods on 22 of 27 tasks. Controlled experiments further show consistent benefits across sensor configurations and EEG-ECG backbone choices, while pretrained initialization outperforms architecture-matched training from scratch and SleepXA surpasses alternative multimodal composition strategies. These results suggest that synchronized multimodal physiology can serve as a natural interface for composing existing physiological foundation models, yielding reusable representations that extend beyond sleep to clinical and daytime physiological settings.
authors: Xiaoyu Chen, Xiao Gu, Chao Zhang

title: Is the learner or the summary the limit? Auditing machine-learning energy reconstruction for air-shower arrays on KASCADE and GRAPES-3
abstract: Machine-learning energy estimators for cosmic-ray arrays are usually trained on a few fitted shower parameters, not station signals. When their resolution stops improving, standard diagnostics cannot say whether a better model would help or the summary has run out of information. We use a five-step audit that compares trained models with a learner-independent estimate of the lowest error the summary allows (its squared-loss Bayes risk, or floor), tests which inputs add information and flags inputs merely computed from the fit. We apply it to public KASCADE simulations with three hadronic-interaction models (QGSJET-II-04, EPOS-LHC and SIBYLL-2.3d), to 13,848,509 measured KASCADE events and to simulated GRAPES-3 events. Within known energy decades below 10^16 eV, gradient boosting on nine reconstructed features is within 2.2% of the estimated floor under every estimator setting, so more capacity is not expected to gain more than about 2%. The floor is an estimate, accurate to about 1% in a semi-synthetic benchmark with intervals that under-cover, and not a bound on the true Bayes risk. Replacing reconstructed by true particle numbers removes 70 to 72% of the error variance below 10^15 eV and 24 to 26% between 10^16 and 10^17 eV on all three models, yet simulated station signals close about a tenth of that gap. On GRAPES-3, networks given images rendered from the fit do no better than the fit. In measured data, the mean muon size at fixed electron size lies within every model's proton-to-iron bracket and a label-free probe finds the muon channel used as in simulation; neither fixes the energy scale. Energy-labelled results are simulated.
authors: Mugdha Raje Ashiya, Samarjeet Malik

title: Hybrid state-space and attention neural operators for nonlinear structural dynamics under environmental loading
abstract: The computational burden of repeated nonlinear time-history analyses limits their application for structural assessment and design. We therefore propose DeepOJamba, a hybrid neural operator that combines selective state-space recurrence with full attention to predict the structural response history due to dynamic loading. Physical-parameter conditioning and predicted-state transfer between sequences enable a single trained operator to represent varying system conditions and generate response histories beyond its training sequence length. DeepOJamba is evaluated on a 15~MW monopile offshore wind turbine under wind and wave loading. The proposed operator is compared to pure attention, pure state-space, Fourier, and DeepONet operators and is found to give the lowest window error on every channel and the lowest closed-loop fatigue and ultimate-load errors of $9.4\%$ and $6.0\%$, against $14.6\%$ and $8.7\%$ for the next-best pure attention operator examined. Moreover, on sea states outside the training wave band, the error slightly increases by approximately $0.4$ percentage points. Pure state-space operators can approach similar low errors only with a much wider convolution kernel tuned to the tower eigenperiod, which increases the training cost by $40\%$. In all, the results obtained support hybrid neural operators for robust long-duration structural response and demand prediction.
authors: Anastasios Stamou, Rui Teixeira, Maria Nogal

title: Reward Tilting via Semantic Noising
abstract: Steering a generative model toward a desired property typically requires separate fine-tuning for each reward or additional computation during sampling. We propose semantic noising, which conditions generation on a noisy semantic representation of the data. The resulting posteriors correspond to exponential tilts by linear-quadratic rewards in semantic space, allowing a single model to support objectives and strengths chosen after training. A conditional generator can be trained to approximate these posteriors directly, while models that generate semantic representations by diffusion provide analytic tilted denoisers for the same family of rewards. We illustrate semantic noising in three settings. An autoregressive molecular generator trained with semantic noising controls properties individually and jointly, with a better reward--KL trade-off than property-conditioned models. On ImageNet, a joint diffusion model of images and their CLIP embeddings achieves FID comparable to REG, and tilting it toward a higher aesthetic score matches the best of 16 samples at the cost of a single sample. Finally, pretrained factorized models such as Kandinsky 2.2 support the same tilts without retraining.
authors: Rafał Karczewski, Peter Blohm, Markus Heinonen

title: Compared to What? Calibrating Machine-Unlearning Diagnostics with Present, Absent and Suppressed Anchors
abstract: Unlearning methods for language models are judged mainly by behaviour, but a model can stop producing an answer while still encoding it. Internal diagnostics such as linear probes, the logit lens and relearning speed are used to tell removal from suppression, yet none has been checked against cases where the answer is known. We build such cases. A present anchor learned a set of synthetic facts; an absent anchor is a never-taught oracle retrained without them; and suppressed anchors are unlearned with their lower layers frozen, so the facts stay encoded below the frozen block by construction. We compare these anchors with NPO, RMU and gradient difference at a matched operating point on GPT-2 Small and Qwen3-0.6B-Base, scoring every diagnostic per entity with AUROC against the oracle. Behaviour cannot separate the suppressed anchors from the oracle (AUROC 0.51 to 0.58), while probes, the logit lens and relearning gain can (0.65 to 1.00), and the oracle seeds stay near 0.5. Applied to NPO on both models and RMU on Qwen3, the validated diagnostics disagree: probes put the facts at the oracle's level, while the models still relearn them much faster than a never-taught model does. Every unlearned model, anchor or method, also assigns the forgotten answer a far lower log-probability than the oracle does, a black-box signal that flagged all of them. A drift-ratio specificity rule fails on known cases. Code, data and every run are at https://github.com/ArsalanKaleem/unlearning-audit.
authors: Arsalan Kaleem

title: $ζ_0$: A Framework for World Action Models with Joint Scene and Body Foresight in Humanoid Control
abstract: World Action Models anticipate visual outcomes to guide robot actions, yet humanoid interaction also depends on how the robot's body responds. Visual foresight alone can miss body motion, while latent-distance losses do not directly supervise action responses. We present $ζ_0$, a framework that turns vision-language-action policies into World Action Models by foreseeing future visual features and measured joint trajectories in a shared latent representation. During training, a teacher conditioned on recorded futures provides a reference action response, and dual-response transfer trains the causal predictor to match it through the teacher and the executing policy. All components are trained jointly, and deployment uses only causally predicted futures. On seven HumanoidArena tasks, $ζ_0$ built on $Ψ_0$ and GR00T N1.7 reaches 63.6% and 79.5% mean success, 18.8 and 9.0 points above these bases. On six real-world tasks, it reaches 78.3% and 85.0%, gains of 16.7 and 10.0 points. On GR00T, its 79.5% tops all compared seven-task joint policies. Project page: https://chenyizhi123.github.io/zeta0-project/
authors: Yizhi Chen, Zhanxiang Cao, Yitong Wang

title: A comparison of knot point screening algorithms for highly adaptive lasso
abstract: Highly adaptive lasso (HAL) is a nonparametric regression estimator with a rate of convergence $n^{-1/3}(\log n)^{d/2}$, where the data dimension $d$ only appears in the power of the log of sample size. This fast rate is crucial for many causal inference tasks, where efficient estimation typically requires nuisance parameters to be estimated at a specific rate. HAL achieves this rate and, when paired with semiparametrically efficient estimators -- such as those constructed using targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) -- can be used to develop efficient estimators. Beyond causal inference, HAL is applicable to a wide range of supervised machine learning tasks. The procedure for HAL involves first performing a basis expansion on the original design matrix $X$ and then computing a lasso solution path. Cross-validation is used to select the optimal $L_1$-norm for the coefficients. For datasets with all continuous covariates and no ties, the HAL design matrix can reach a dimension as large as $n \times n(2^d-1)$, imposing a significant computational and memory burden. To address this, screening algorithms are applied at both the variable and knot-point levels to make HAL practical for datasets of moderate to large sizes. In this work, we propose outcome-blind knot point screening based on center-based clustering -- $k$-means and partitioning around medoids (PAM) -- and compare it with the quantile-based screening implemented in the hal9001 R package at matched design-matrix sizes. Across 153 simulation settings, $k$-means and PAM significantly improved test $R^2$ in 97 and 111 settings, respectively, with gains that grow with covariate skewness, while producing slightly smaller design matrices. On nine real-world datasets, they reduced the cross-validated mean squared error by 35-36% on the dataset with the most skewed predictors and performed comparably on the others.
authors: Yadi Weng, Sky Qiu

title: Benchmarking Web Agent Defenses Against Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection
abstract: Multimodal web agents automate website interactions but remain vulnerable to visual prompt injection (VPI), where malicious webpage content manipulates their visual processing and induces unintended actions. Although several defenses focus on detecting injected instructions in screenshots, malicious destinations such as phishing URLs embedded in HTML can remain hidden yet accessible through agent interactions. Existing evaluations have also not sufficiently examined adaptive attackers who know the defense mechanisms. To address these limitations, we introduce AdaptiveVPI, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating adaptive VPI threats in web agents. Specifically, we present a dataset of 360 webpage instances spanning 6 distinct hijack strategies across 10 real-world websites, with malicious destinations not visible in screenshots. We design an adaptive attack framework that iteratively refines malicious instructions based on feedback from the defense mechanism being evaluated. We also introduce three metrics to measure the extent of agent hijacking at three different levels. Across 10 defense configurations for computer-use agents and 11 defense configurations for browser-use agents, our adaptive attacks achieve average success rates of 91.87% and 91.99%, respectively. These results reveal a gap between current VPI defenses and realistic threats and highlight the need for defenses designed with adaptive attackers in mind.
authors: Haichuan Zhang, Zhiyuan Zhong, Shih-Chieh Dai

title: OAT3D: A Generative Model for 3D Shape- and Resolution-Free Structural Topology Optimization
abstract: Topology optimization determines how material should be distributed within a design domain to optimize structural performance under prescribed loads, supports, and constraints. The problems are highly nonconvex, and conventional solvers require repeated finite element analyses, making high-resolution 3D topology optimization computationally expensive. Data-driven approaches face an additional bottleneck: generating training datasets requires solving large numbers of these costly problems, so existing work in data-driven topology optimization primarily focuses on 2D problems. Large-scale 3D datasets remain scarce, and existing models remain limited in problem scale and boundary-condition diversity. Here, we introduce Optimize Any Topology-3D (OAT3D), a generative model for high-resolution 3D structural topology optimization. OAT3D introduces a novel sparse problem encoding to represent load and fixity conditions and combines a sparse volumetric variational autoencoder with a conditional diffusion transformer. We construct a dataset of 501,865 optimized topologies, generated using 51,800 GPU-hours and encompassing structures with up to one million elements and substantially more complex loading and support configurations than any existing structural topology optimization dataset. To our knowledge, this is the largest dataset for 3D topology optimization structures. Trained on this dataset, OAT3D generates structures at 512$^3$ resolution and achieves a $44.9\times$ speedup for raw candidate structure generation or $3.65\times$ speedup to reach similar compliance over conventional topology optimization. These contributions expand the scale and diversity of data-driven topology optimization for three-dimensional structural design.
authors: Hongrui Chen, Kittipong Thiamchaiboonthawee, Zhen Wei

title: Zarc: Exact Nearest Neighbors over a Billion Vectors in Seconds
abstract: Exact k-nearest-neighbor vector search lies on the critical path of machine learning systems, from sparse attention in the latest large language models (LLMs) to long-context memories and training-data deduplication. Exhaustive GPU search scans the whole dataset for every query, while approximate indexes return inexact neighbors. Recent methods skip almost every vector with a cheap half-precision proof that it lies too far away, but only on one GPU that holds the whole dataset. Our insight is to keep only the short rows of these proofs in GPU memory and to fetch the few remaining full vectors from host memory. Our system, Zarc, answers Euclidean, cosine, inner-product, and filtered queries exactly under updates. On four H100 GPUs, it answers 10,000 exact queries over one billion vectors in 1.1 seconds instead of five minutes. On eleven open LLMs, it retrieves the exact top-10 attention keys 2.2x to 13.1x faster than exhaustive search. In sparse attention over one million tokens, it runs 3.1x faster than bf16 selection with FlashInfer, which misses the exact top-64 for most queries.
authors: Dongfang Zhao

title: Fuzzy e-Means: Fuzzy c-Means on Large Data with Moving-Average Mini-Batch Updates
abstract: Fuzzy c-means (FCM) gives every point a degree of membership in every cluster. Its standard solver, alternating optimization (AO), needs a full pass over the data per iteration and often many iterations, while methods built for large data stop at a worse objective or still need tens of passes. We run FCM with the optimizer of e-means, a recent mini-batch k-means that keeps moving averages of the number and the sum of the points in each cluster and sets its batch size and step size by scaling laws. The optimizer carries over because an FCM centroid is also a weighted sum divided by a total weight, but this direct transfer fails in two ways: the e-means rule that relocates nearly empty clusters also removes the centroids of small, distant groups, and FCM started from random points can settle in poor local minima. Fuzzy e-means (e-FCM) therefore starts with one pass of e-means with hard assignments and then runs fuzzy moving-average passes without relocation. On 28 configurations with up to 109.5 million points and 16,384 clusters, e-FCM reaches the objective of 25 AO iterations in two to four passes when clusters hold several hundred points or more, 11 to 20 times faster than AO on one-million-point embedding sets with 1,024 clusters. It ends within 0.16% of converged AO on these sets and below converged AO where AO from random points lands in poor minima, but it is slower than AO on small low-dimensional problems, where an AO pass takes milliseconds. Finally, the common fuzzifier m=2 makes the centroids collapse or merge on most high-dimensional sets, and e-FCM can choose the fuzzifier by matching a known overlap at about two passes per candidate value.
authors: Paritosh Tiwari, Punit Rathore

title: Why Adaptive Optimizers Struggle with Large Convolution Kernels
abstract: Large convolution kernels enlarge the receptive fields of ConvNets at a modest computational cost, but they are notoriously difficult to train. Existing large-kernel networks therefore rely on costly training techniques, such as parallel small-kernel branches with batch normalization. In this paper, we trace this difficulty to adaptive optimizers such as Adam, which normalize the update of every weight separately. Since input features rarely average to zero, all weights of a kernel share a common gradient, and these optimizers move the mean of a $k\times k$ kernel $k$ times as far as a single parameter. We find this mean amplification in widely used ConvNets and vision transformers, and show that it can force the maximal learning rate to fall as $1/k^2$. We further prove that the basis of the discrete cosine transform (DCT) isolates the mean and is the only orthonormal basis that diagonalizes every stationary gradient statistic with mirrored boundaries. We therefore train large kernels through their DCT coefficients and convert them back after training. The resulting method, DCT-Rep, requires only a few lines of code and adds no parameters, no inference cost and negligible training overhead. Extensive experiments on image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation and image restoration show that DCT-Rep consistently improves large-kernel ConvNets and vision transformers, by $+0.79\%$ top-1 accuracy for a large-kernel ConvNeXt-T and $+0.43\%$ for ViT-S/16 on ImageNet-1K, $+1.4$ box AP on COCO, $+1.2$ mIoU on ADE20K and up to $+0.4$ dB on image deblurring, where the gain grows with the kernel size.
authors: Tianyu Ding, Jiachen Jiang, Jinxin Zhou

title: Curvature Mismatch and Local Errors in Galaxy Property Estimation
abstract: Linear probes are widely used to evaluate learned representations and infer physical quantities from unlabelled data. The probe's predictions are from an affine function in ambient space restricted to the underlying representation, and consequently, even a representation that has complete information needed to predict a target can produce systematic probe errors when that information is encoded in a form inaccessible to the linear probe. Here we share that some of this probing error is due to the innate geometry of the manifold. Linear probes, when evaluated on a curved manifold, generally have a nonzero intrinsic Hessian (what we colloquially call "probe-facing curvature") given by $\langle w_N,\mathrm{II}\rangle$, the manifold's second fundamental form dotted with the probe's normal component. We fit linear probes to galaxy embeddings from five pretrained encoders and intervene on this curvature term to evaluate its contribution to the probe performance. We find that keeping this inherited curvature improves the local fit where it matches the label's curvature. Removing the curvature component of the probe where it does not match the label curvature also provides improvements, and correcting it in every neighbourhood raises held-out local $R^2$ by 0.006 to 0.010 on galaxies, gaining more where the two curvatures disagree. We isolated these gains to be from the underlying geometry and not an automatic guarantee from least squares training.
authors: Austin Lutterbach, Angus Hoy, Jasper Chong

title: NANO: Unifying Missingness and Input Uncertainty in Tabular Learning
abstract: Missing values are common in tabular data, yet current approaches to handling them often overlook two dimensions. First, an observed value may be uncertain, while a Not-Observed (N.O.) value may still have a reasonable estimate. Inputs should therefore span a continuous spectrum from no evidence to a fully trusted observation. Second, Not-Applicable (N.A.) means that no meaningful value exists for a record, yet this semantic state often lacks explicit representation. To address both dimensions, we introduce NANO, a unified plug-in for input encoding that fits most token-based architectures. Guided by Bayesian evidence weighting, NANO adjusts the influence of a supplied value according to confidence, with all zero-confidence estimates mapped to the same N.O. representation. NANO accepts, but does not require, per-example confidence information during training or inference. For N.A., a separate representation enables models to encode inapplicability and its schema-defined reasons into context. Experiments across eleven datasets and nine backbones show that mixed-confidence training enables a single NANO model to generalize across inference confidence levels, remaining competitive without estimates and improving steadily as estimate reliability and confidence increase. The effectiveness of NANO's handling of N.A. is further demonstrated on three augmented datasets.
authors: Kuangdai Leng, Maria Tsekhmistrenko, Matteo Bagagli

title: THETA: Heat Diffusion as a Structural Prior for Cross-Domain Transfer in Graph Foundation Models
abstract: Graph foundation models (GFMs) aim to learn transferable representations across domains with heterogeneous node attributes and graph structures. However, relations inferred from node attributes can rely on domain-specific feature semantics, limiting their transferability to unseen graphs, particularly in low-label regimes. We propose THETA (Topology-aware HEat-based TrAnsfer), a graph foundation model that leverages Heat Kernel Signatures (HKS) as a topology-based structural prior for cross-domain transfer. By characterizing nodes' heat-return behavior across diffusion scales, HKS provides a common structural descriptor across graphs without requiring aligned attribute semantics, complementing feature-based relations with information about local and multiscale connectivity. THETA incorporates this prior into both pre-training and few-shot adaptation. During pre-training, it combines HKS with node attributes to construct refined graph views and trains a shared encoder via contrastive learning. During adaptation, it uses HKS to guide edge-weight adjustment and prototype refinement while keeping the encoder frozen and retaining the contribution of labeled support nodes. Through HKS, THETA uses structural information from heat diffusion to guide both representation learning and few-shot adaptation with unlabeled target-domain data. Extensive experiments across diverse graph domains demonstrate that THETA consistently outperforms existing baselines on downstream tasks, highlighting the value of heat diffusion as a structural prior for transferable graph representations.
authors: Haonan Liu, Shuo Wang, Zhao Kang

title: Ziv Meets Sumcheck: Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Floating-Point LLM Inference
abstract: Zero-knowledge proofs can show that a neural network produced a given output without revealing the network, but current systems for language models prove integer approximations of the model rather than the floating-point arithmetic that is actually deployed. Proving floating-point matrix multiplication has been regarded as hard, because rounding after every addition makes the result depend on the order of the additions. We avoid this obstacle by proving the correctly rounded product, in which every dot product is computed exactly and rounded once. This result is independent of the hardware and at least as accurate as standard kernels. We give an interactive proof for this relation whose cost is close to that of integer matrix multiplication, with roughly a thousand times fewer committed values than per-operation floating-point circuits need constraints, extend it to every layer of a transformer, and give a privacy construction for the complete argument whose zero knowledge we prove under explicit hypotheses. We implement the system and prove the full forward pass of GPT-2 small, including all twelve blocks and the output over the whole vocabulary, in 19 minutes on two processor cores; verification takes 21 seconds. The verifier rejects all 236 attacks we tested, and the model's outputs agree with high-precision inference at least as closely as standard 16-bit inference does.
authors: Hassan Khodaiemehr, Khadijeh Bagheri, Chen Feng

title: ARC: Adaptive Rollout Control for Efficient Synchronous LLM Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Synchronous reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models proceeds through a repeated rollout--barrier--update loop. Each update must wait for a fixed number of complete, group-relative training samples, yet individual response lengths and reward outcomes vary widely and only emerge as generation progresses. Static admission and unconditional completion therefore leave accelerators idle in some steps, and waste computation generating samples that will never contribute to the current update. We present ARC, a closed-loop rollout architecture that governs synchronous RL rollout at group granularity. ARC uses \textit{Calibrated Streaming Backfill} to judge from partial observations whether a group is still worth completing, backfilling a fresh candidate immediately when it is not; \textit{Deferred Group Completion} to park an uncertain early stop and resume it later instead of discarding it outright, bounded by a resume-cycle limit that guarantees termination; and \textit{Adaptive Admission} and \textit{Pipelining} to order admitted samples by early-measured duration and to admit further candidates only while expected supply still falls short of the target number of accepted groups. Under online evaluation, ARC reduces rollout time by $37.4\%$, a $1.60\times$ speedup, and improves effective GRPO throughput by $50.1\%$ over existing baselines, while directly recovering 98.9\% of the training groups that would ultimately have been kept.
authors: Yihui Zhang, Tianyu Wo, Jinghao Wang

title: ATLAS: Autoregressive Trajectories for Longitudinal Analysis of Survival
abstract: Dynamic survival prediction requires estimates that reflect a patient's observed clinical history. We introduce ATLAS (Autoregressive Trajectories for Longitudinal Analysis of Survival), a framework that trains a sequence model on longitudinal data and autoregressively samples possible futures conditional on an individual's covariates and observed history. These trajectories form a patient-specific synthetic cohort from which Kaplan-Meier survival curves and Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence curves are estimated. We evaluate ATLAS using two stochastic finite-state automaton benchmarks with exact conditional reference curves: a single-covariate process with duration dependence and a late rule change, and a three-covariate Markov process with recovery and competing causes of death. Comparisons include eight direct survival models, including validation-optimized DRSA and Dynamic-DeepHit and history-aware SurvTRACE adaptations, with each neural model trained nine times in the first experiment and five times in the second. After baseline, every ATLAS configuration had lower mean survival-curve error than every fitted direct comparator in both experiments. With a common Sobol sampler and 10,000 trajectories per patient, the best ATLAS model did so in every individual training run, and its mean error was 62% to 84% lower than that of the strongest direct comparator. Baseline advantages were smaller and less consistent in the duration-dependent experiment. ATLAS provides a generative framework for history-conditioned survival estimation, while the accompanying benchmarks enable direct assessment of individual survival and competing-risk predictions against known reference curves.
authors: Morgan Nissen, Chunyang Li, Seth Glazier

title: Towards Edge Artificial Intelligence for Predicting Antimicrobial Resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) poses a major challenge to global tuberculosis control, as multidrug-resistant strains limit available treatment options. Rapid and accurate prediction of drug resistance from genomic data could support timely treatment decisions and public health interventions. However, many existing computational approaches for genomic AMR prediction rely on computationally intensive pipelines, limiting their suitability for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. This limitation is particularly relevant in hospital settings in low- and middle-income countries, where computing infrastructure and access to high-performance computational resources may be limited. To address this challenge, we present a lightweight, novel machine learning (ML) approach suitable for running on edge devices that combines 4-mer frequency features derived from whole-genome sequences with a Random Forest classifier to predict antibiotic resistance in MTB. The proposed ML approach achieved an average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.82 across 20 antibiotics on an independent test set.
authors: Nishat Tasnim, Faisal Ahmed, Rokan Uddin Faruqui

title: Handover Cost Optimization in LEO Satellite Networks using an RL-based Multiple-Column Selection Strategy via Branch-and-Price
abstract: Next-generation wireless networks increasingly rely on low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites for broad coverage and low latency, making efficient handover management essential. We formulate satellite handover as a combinatorial optimization problem, assigning each ground user to exactly one capacity-limited, visible satellite while minimizing network handover costs. We propose a reinforcement learning (RL)-based branch-and-price (B&P) framework with learned multiple-column selection (MCS) to accelerate column generation while retaining exact dynamic programming pricing. We also develop two lightweight heuristic policies: handover-aware visibility duration (HAVD) for online decisions and congestion-aware predictive (CAP) for offline planning. Additionally, a local-search repair algorithm adapts precomputed B&P or MCS-B&P solutions to demand perturbations through single-flip and per-user trajectory re-optimization, avoiding complete re-optimization. Simulations using realistic large scale constellations, including Starlink Gen-1, demonstrate that MCS-B&P achieves solution quality comparable to exact B&P with fewer column-generation iterations, fewer branch-and-bound nodes, and reduced computation time. HAVD and CAP offer effective online and offline cost-latency trade-offs, while local-search repair recovers most performance losses due to demand perturbations at a fraction of the computational cost of full re-optimization.
authors: Mandar R. Nalavade, Gaurav S. Kasbekar, Koushik Kar

title: Pain Reassessment from Pulse Waveforms with Language Model Explanations
abstract: Routine photoplethysmography (PPG) offers a continuous physiological signal for pain reassessment between self-reports. Whether prior recordings provide an individualized physiological reference beyond care-process timing remains unresolved. Across 52,082 report-linked assessments from 21,514 patients in MIMIC-III critical care and MC-MED emergency care, we evaluate a workflow that pairs longitudinal PPG representations with local evidence-linked language interpretation. Among 27 methods, source-selected full-history models achieved average precision of 0.824 from critical to emergency care and 0.822 in reverse. Removing historical pulse-run representations while retaining reassessment availability and elapsed time lowered critical-to-emergency four-hour within-patient concordance from 0.718 to 0.534. This comparison supports the contribution of prior pulse-run representations to within-patient ordering beyond timing cues. Across 2,905 test patients, a local Qwen model interpreting frozen predictions achieved a 94.7% patient-equal pass rate on automated evidence checks after at most one revision. Longitudinal pulse context and evidence-linked language interpretation support a patient-centred workflow for pain reassessment.
authors: Cheng Ding, Jiaming Liu, Daoqiang Zhang

title: DUO Policy: Bridging Human Video Coverage and Robot Precision for Fine-Grained Manipulation
abstract: Human videos promise a scalable way to reduce expensive robot data collection, but the embodiment gap limits the resulting policies to coarse behaviors, and they fail at precise tasks such as insertion. Existing methods co-train or finetune a single policy on both data sources, treating each source as equally useful in every state: the policy either absorbs the embodiment error at precision-critical steps or spends scarce robot data relearning free-space motion. We observe that the value of each source depends on the state: human data is useful where precision requirements are low, while robot data is disproportionately valuable near precision-critical states. We therefore propose \textbf{DUO Policy} (Dual-Actor Policy), which decouples a manipulation skill into a hand policy, pretrained on human videos for global free-space motion, and a robot policy, trained on sparse in-hand data for local precise corrections, with a gate learned from human interventions switching between them. This design is robust to moderate embodiment error in human data and generalizes to scene layouts beyond the coverage of the robot data. On tasks such as K-cup coffee making, desk cleanup, and cluttered candy sorting, DUO Policy outperforms the baseline with the highest average success by 12.9 percentage points over four simulated tasks and by 51.7 points over three real-world tasks, and matches robot-only training with 2.75$\times$ less data-collection time. Project Webpage: https://mingxi-jia.github.io/duo_policy_site/
authors: Mingxi Jia, Patton Jiyang Yin, Haojie Huang

title: Neural Costate Guidance for Autonomous Cislunar Low-Thrust Trajectory Generation
abstract: Future missions will benefit from onboard autonomous low-thrust trajectory generation to correct deviations from the nominal flight path caused by navigation errors and thruster outages. Onboard computing resources rarely allow the solution of a cold-started, long-duration nonconvex optimal control problem, especially in dynamically challenging regions such as the cislunar to translunar corridor of the Earth-Moon system. This paper develops data augmentation and training techniques that enable a neural network to predict accurate initial costates of the indirect method. A recovery trajectory is then built from repeated network queries in a computationally efficient guidance algorithm. Training data are produced by the backward generation of optimal examples method, extending prior approaches to the circular restricted three-body problem. A novel anchor trajectory approach is developed to cover the relevant state space, and costate rescaling and a Hamiltonian loss term are used to improve learning. The method is demonstrated on Earth-Moon transfers from a high Earth orbit to halo orbits about L1 and L2. Under navigation errors and thruster outages, a spacecraft reaches the target orbit more often with the proposed method than with nominal-trajectory tracking or fully numerical reoptimization. Onboard computation is reduced by more than an order of magnitude compared with reoptimization.
authors: Jannik Graebner, Ryne Beeson

title: HME-PFD: Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Privileged Feature Distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models, facilitating efficient serving of machine learning systems. In the context of ads recommendation, privileged features distillation (PFD) extends KD by allowing the teacher model to leverage privileged features, i.e., features available only during training, to enhance distillation performance. However, in real-world scenarios, privileged features often have limited coverage and exhibit heterogeneous distributions, resulting in training examples of varying importance for distillation and model learning. We propose Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Privileged Feature Distillation (HME-PFD), a novel approach that incorporates privileged features into the routing module of a Mixture-of-Experts-based student model. Our method introduces both hard-coded and learnable routing modules, enabling the student to dynamically determine expert assignment based on the availability and values of privileged features. This design allows the student model to better handle the heterogeneous data scenario, where privileged features are partially observed, by differentiating between high- and low-signal samples. Extensive experiments on two post-click conversion prediction tasks demonstrate that HME-PFD consistently outperforms baseline methods. Our results show that leveraging privileged features for expert routing in the student model leads to improved model performance, even when privileged features are incomplete or sparse.
authors: Wen Xu, Xiaomin Zhang, Yucheng Yang

title: TrustFlow-ECG: Reliability-Aware ECG Restoration with Calibrated Risk Estimation
abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) restoration models can reduce noise and motion artifacts, but they rarely estimate whether the restored waveform is reliable for downstream analysis. We propose TrustFlow-ECG, a reliability-aware restoration framework that combines a one-step conditional rectified-flow restorer with a lightweight window-level risk predictor.
