What appears to be routine hyperparameter tuning is in fact a normative choice about whose preferences define quality.
authors: David Gamba, Seura Ha, Daniel M. Romero

title: DRAM: Memory-Efficient Muon via Rank Reallocation in Principal-Random Subspaces
abstract: Memory-efficient Muon methods aim to reduce storage overhead while preserving strong performance, yet existing approaches compromise either convergence guarantees or practical efficiency. In this paper, we focus on subspace optimization for Muon, where the choice of subspace determines the gradient information retained for updating. To preserve dominant information while providing the coverage needed for stochastic convergence guarantees, we construct a principal-random subspace that combines leading singular directions of the stochastic gradient with random directions sampled from their orthogonal complement. Under a fixed rank budget, there is a trade-off between principal exploitation and complementary coverage, making rank allocation important for practical optimization. Our key observation is that the preferred balance shifts from principal-heavy early in training to random-heavy later. Motivated by this shift, we propose \dram, a memory-efficient Muon optimizer that reallocates principal and random ranks across stages while maintaining momentum and performing matrix-sign normalization entirely in the subspace. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for general rank-allocation schedules with nondecreasing coverage factors, obtaining rates of $O(T^{-1/4})$ in the stochastic setting and $O(T^{-1/2})$ in the deterministic setting, with fixed allocation as a special case. Using a simple linear reallocation schedule, \dram achieves the best low-memory performance across three pre-training scales and nine fine-tuning settings.
authors: Haomin Bai, Dingzhi Yu, Xuling Zhao

title: Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
abstract: We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution $μ$, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When $μ$ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When $μ$ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured $O(d\log T)$ mistake bound; When $μ$ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in $T$ and in terms of the VC dimension $d$, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an $O(\sqrt{dT})$ balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to $\operatorname{poly}(dD\log T)$ factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension $D$. Our guarantees also extend to censored feedback, where the label is hidden after an abstention.
authors: Moïse Blanchard, Ezra Edelman, Surbhi Goel

title: Complex band-limited maximum likelihood: estimating the wave behind detected quanta
abstract: Detected photons and electrons land at positions drawn from $|ψ|^2$, yet it is $ψ$, phase included, that a wave equation propagates, and the state that produced the particles is often known only in part. A density estimator can recover $|ψ|^2$ directly from the positions, without any wave equation, but it discards the phase, and with it the state. We introduce complex band-limited maximum likelihood (complex BLML), which estimates $ψ$ itself by maximising the likelihood of the detected positions over exactly the intensities the physics allows: squared moduli of complex functions whose spectrum lies in a given set, such as a band, the shape of the aperture, or several modes for a partially coherent source. A single eigenvalue can certify a global maximum. On simulated two-slit far fields we measure what each prior is worth: a band reaches a given accuracy with seven times fewer photons than a kernel density estimate and already gives the fringe contrast and the relative phase, and the shape of the aperture adds the slit geometry. Some quantities need a prior at any number of photons: for slits of one profile the intensity fixes only the contrast $2ρV/(1+ρ^2)$, and on a line two different apertures can produce the same particles. Cutting a pattern to a few fringes, as published records are, removes the slit width. On four public single-particle double-slit records it predicts held-out particles best among the methods we tested, kernel estimators and two-slit optical models included, and it recovers the fringe contrast without a model of the optics. On fluorescent beads it finds the resolution limit of the microscope, $2\mathrm{NA}/λ$, from the photons alone.
authors: Rahul Agarwal, Ankit Agarwal

title: When and Where to Transfer: Learning Transferable Historical Contexts for Short-History Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Related sources can improve multivariate time series forecasting when the target history is short, but their usefulness varies across source groups and historical periods. A key challenge is to identify informative historical contexts from the sources. This paper proposes Hierarchical Context Transfer (HiCT), a framework that adaptively weights source groups and their historical contexts to determine both \emph{where} and \emph{when} to transfer. A shared context encoder and cross-attention are used to learn weights over source groups and historical contexts. These weights guide regularized transfer estimation, followed by an optional target-specific correction. This paper establishes a target excess-risk bound for the context-weighted transfer estimator. Experiments demonstrate competitive predictive performance across four multivariate forecasting datasets and a favorable accuracy--runtime trade-off against the evaluated baselines. Source-corruption ablations illustrate the roles of group-level and within-group weighting in adapting to unreliable source histories.
authors: Huiling Yuan, Yize Wang, Guodong Li

title: Shoonya: Zero-Socket In-Process Small Language Models for Graph Databases with Schema-Epoch KV Caching, Live Catalog Logit Masking, and Verifier-Advantage Distillation
abstract: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. We present Shoonya, from-scratch commercially clean (0.0% non-commercial or share-alike data) tri-modal (Python, Rust, OpenCypher) small language models (16.8M to 1.07B parameters) co-designed with shoonya-infer, a zero-dependency pure-Rust runtime embedded inside the samyama-graph-enterprise address space. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x--13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8--67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed ($α\in [1.88, 2.20]$). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1--v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.
authors: Madhulatha Mandarapu, Sandeep Kunkunuru

title: An equivariant classical density functional for ionic fluids at complex interfaces
abstract: Predicting the combined effects of ionic packing and long-range electrostatics at complex interfaces is technologically important, but remains challenging without atomistic simulations. Here we present a machine-learned classical density functional for ionic fluids that combines a symmetry-adapted neural free energy for short-range correlations with explicit long-range electrostatics. Trained on three-dimensional equilibrium densities and bulk correlations of the full-Coulomb restricted primitive model, a single functional transfers to charge-patterned particles and atomically structured electrodes. Around anisotropic charged solutes, it reproduces the ionic structure and mean forces from molecular dynamics, including reversals of the bare electrostatic force. At metal electrodes, self-consistent coupling to metal atoms captures the redistribution of ionic and electrode charge and the loading-dependent capacitance enhancement produced by steps and bumps. Combined with mobilities determined independently from bulk molecular dynamics, the same functional describes the main features of charging dynamics and resolves geometry-dependent spatial relaxation. This framework can be extended to more complex ionic fluids, enabling efficient exploration of how composition and geometry control structure and response.
authors: Bingqing Cheng

title: Accelerating wave-scattering simulations with learned search directions
abstract: Wave-scattering simulation requires solving a dense boundary-element system for every frequency, incidence and design. Krylov solvers build each search space from scratch, and it grows with problem size. Here we present BEMFormer, a solver that learns to generate search directions across systems of one integral equation and supplies geometry-specific directions through a coarse-grid correction. BEMFormer generalizes to unseen geometries, meshes and excitations, and to acoustic scattering after fine-tuning on eight geometries. It reproduces the measured radar cross-sections of benchmark targets. On a quadcopter with 1.04 million unknowns, 38 times the largest training problem, BEMFormer solves each system 30 times faster than a preconditioned Krylov solver. Both reach a radar cross-section deviation of about 1 dB, comparable to the difference between independent measurements and acceptable for engineering applications. These results show that solving million-unknown scattering problems in minutes is possible when the search space is learned rather than built from scratch.
authors: Haoran Sun, Tao Shan, Hongyu Zhou

title: AMP-OD: Active Model Probing for Unsupervised Outlier Model Selection--Extended Version
abstract: Outlier detection is often deployed in fully unsupervised settings, where labels are unavailable and practitioners must choose a detector without direct performance feedback. Existing unsupervised outlier model selection methods predict detector quality from static meta-features and historical performance on meta-datasets, but they commit before observing how any detector behaves on the target dataset. We propose AMP-OD, an execution-conditioned probe-then-commit framework. AMP-OD runs a small number of inexpensive probe detectors, uses their score patterns as target-dataset evidence, and then selects a final detector from a larger candidate pool. To interpret unlabeled probe responses, we introduce a Leave-One-Out Family Probe Posterior (LOO-FPP), which converts probe score patterns into gated detector-family evidence while reducing self-validation in pseudo-label construction. AMP-OD further combines this evidence with historical reliability through a warm-start prior, a sequential probe/stop policy, and lower-confidence-bound arbitration. Extensive experiments and ablation studies show that detector responses provide useful evidence beyond static meta-features, with the LOO-FPP and conservative arbitration as key contributors.
authors: Hong-Phuc Phan, Tuan-Anh Vu, Tung Kieu

title: A hybrid Graph-based Machine Learning Model for predicting Delivery Times in Supply Chain Logistics
abstract: Global supply chains are increasingly vulnerable to disruptions arising from external events, such as natural disasters and geopolitical crises, and from internal operational inefficiencies, including supplier delays and bottlenecks in order shipping. This work, conducted within the Horizon Europe project M4ESTRO, introduces a hybrid modelling approach combining graph theory and machine learning to represent supply chain logistics operations, with a focus on predicting delays in inbound flows between industrial suppliers and manufacturing entities. The various stages of order fulfilment are modelled through a formal mathematical framework, by defining disruption indicators computed from both historical and real-time data drawn from heterogeneous sources, including traffic and weather conditions and supplier dispatch readiness. Building on a graph-based representation of the supply chain, stochastic methods based on Markov chains are applied to estimate delivery times, detect schedule deviations, quantify prediction uncertainty, and produce interpretable metrics to support operational decision-making. Within the M4ESTRO project, the proposed framework was applied to build a web application for real-time tracking of inbound logistics, and was validated in a use case with an industrial project partner. The web application successfully enabled early detection of logistics disruptions along the supply chain and provided stakeholders with the visibility needed to act before delays propagated. The underlying model proved effective as the basis of a resilient, data-driven logistics tracking system, aligned with the digital transformation objectives of industry and with Manufacturing-as-a-Service paradigms.
authors: Mattia Volpato, Andrea Giuseppe Landella, Bruno Puzzolante

title: Optimal User-Level Private Stochastic Convex Optimization and Mean Estimation with Heavy Tails
abstract: We study stochastic convex optimization with heavy-tailed stochastic gradients under $(\varepsilon, δ)$-user-level differential privacy, which protects each user's entire collection of samples. Instead of assuming a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, we only assume bounds on the second- and $k$-th moments of the random sample Lipschitz parameters. This allows for unbounded, heavy-tailed stochastic gradient distributions and can lead to sharper excess risk bounds. We characterize the minimax optimal excess population risk up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm achieves the optimal rate with only $\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ users. As a byproduct of our algorithmic developments, we obtain tight bounds for user-level private mean estimation under norm-moment assumptions, improving over the guarantees of Esfandiari et al. (2022) and Zhao et al. (2024). Finally, for mean estimation under the directional-moment assumption of Agarwal et al. (2025), we close their remaining approximate-DP gap by removing the additional $d/\varepsilon$ user requirement and attaining the optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.
authors: Andrew Lowy

title: When a Permitted Action Completes a Forbidden Workflow: Designing Consequence-Oriented Approval for LLM Agents
abstract: Tool-using language-model agents increasingly ask people to approve consequential actions, yet an approval prompt shows only the next step. A request to send a file to an approved recipient can look harmless even when that file was assembled, several steps earlier, from data the user said must never leave. We call this a cumulative authorization failure and argue that it is an interaction design problem as much as a security problem. The evidence a reviewer needs is spread across the trajectory, and listing it in time order leaves the reviewer to reconstruct the causal chain. We present the Cumulative Consent Ledger (CCL), an approval interface built on four design principles that restate the user's intent, bind the review to the exact action, compose the cumulative consequence, and keep every claim checkable. A trusted monitor that tracks artifact lineage supplies the evidence. In a between-subjects study with 80 participants and 960 approval decisions, CCL was associated with fewer unsafe approvals than an evidence-matched chronological log (24.2% vs. 32.5%), higher comprehension, and faster decisions, although the adjusted difference in unsafe approvals remained uncertain (-7.9 points, 95% CrI [-19.7, 3.8]). In a system evaluation, the monitor detected 89.2% of 120 violating checkpoints and, used as an execution gate, reduced executed unsafe effects from 43.3% to 5.0% for one agent at a small cost to benign completion. We derive implications for designing consent around consequences rather than individual calls.
authors: S M Asif Hossain, Ruksat Khan Shayoni, Md Kishor Morol

title: PFN-Syn: Generating Synthetic Tabular Data with Prior-Data Fitted Networks
abstract: Synthetic tabular data can help enable data sharing and model development in privacy-sensitive domains, but existing generators often require dataset-specific training and substantial computation. We introduce PFN-Syn, a training-free framework for synthetic tabular data generation based on prior-data fitted networks. We evaluate PFN-Syn against training-based generators on eight binary classification datasets. PFN-Syn achieves the highest average downstream utility among evaluated synthetic generators, with higher generation throughput than training-based baselines, while maintaining competitive distributional similarity and distance-to-closest-record privacy behavior. Our results suggest that tabular foundation models can serve as useful building blocks for practical synthetic tabular data generation.
authors: Michael Zuo, Inwon Kang, Oshani Seneviratne

title: Targeted Learning for Externally Controlled Trials and Beyond
abstract: This paper focuses on externally controlled trials (ECTs), which consist of a single-arm clinical trial supplemented by an external control arm (ECA). Potential data sources for the ECA can be broadly classified into three categories: (i) the control arm of a historical clinical trial, (ii) a concurrent cohort study, and (iii) external real-world data (RWD). In this paper, we consider a broad class of estimands defined through balancing weights. For a given estimand in the class, we discuss the efficient influence function (EIF) and the targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE), together with practical implementation algorithms. Within the targeted learning framework, TMLE is a substitution estimator that enjoys several desirable theoretical properties and favorable finite-sample performance. Finally, the proposed framework is extended to two additional settings: (1) randomized controlled trials (RCTs) augmented with external covariate information to define a target population, and (2) indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) that combine individual patient data (IPD) from an internal RCT with aggregate data (AgD) from an external RCT.
authors: Yixin Fang, Weili He

title: Data-Dependent Probability Estimation via Sample Amplification
abstract: Can we estimate the probability of an event chosen after seeing the data, without using any fresh samples? Its empirical probability can be arbitrarily misleading, while learning the entire distribution to constant accuracy requires $Θ(d)$ samples on a domain of size $d$. We show that $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d})$ samples suffice for constant mean squared error, provided the rule choosing the event is known. More generally, our estimator handles arbitrary $[0,1]$-valued queries and runs in polynomial time given evaluation access to the rule. This sample complexity matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors and resolves the open question posed by Feldman, Kale, Raman, Talwar, and Tewari (arXiv:2610.41244). Our estimation framework relies on a new combination of sample amplification (arXiv:1904.12053 and arXiv:2201.04315) with distribution learning via online optimization. Our estimator achieves mean squared error $O(d^{3/4}/n)$ when $d\leq n$ and $\widetilde{O}(d^{1/4}/\sqrt{n})$ when $d>n$. We complement this with a lower bound of $Ω(\min\{1,\sqrt{d}/n\})$ on the mean squared error. Using our framework, we also design an efficient estimator for data-dependent queries on Gaussian distributions with unknown mean and identity covariance. Finally, we show that a smoothed variant of the problem is much (exponentially) easier. For discrete distributions, if the sample size is chosen uniformly from $\{n,\ldots,2n-1\}$, then $n=O(\log d)$ suffices for constant mean squared error.
authors: Vitaly Feldman, Satyen Kale, Mahbod Majid

title: Expressive Shallow Networks for Physics-Informed Learning: Why Curvature-Aware Optimization and FP64 Are Not Enough
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often struggle with high-frequency and high-order partial differential equations (PDEs) due to optimization stiffness and spectral bias, despite possessing sufficient approximation capacity. Existing remedies, including modified feature representations, domain decomposition, higher floating-point precision, and curvature-aware optimizers, can improve convergence but largely act as workarounds for optimization difficulties arising from deep architectures rather than addressing their underlying source. We investigate Physics-Informed Shallow Universal Polynomial Networks (PI-SUPNs), which replace deep nonlinear compositions with learnable polynomial expansions, retaining high approximation capacity within a shallow computational graph. On a high-frequency Helmholtz benchmark, PI-SUPNs are the only architecture to successfully recover the solution, while all competing models fail even under FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization. However, experiments on higher vibrational modes of a fourth-order Euler-Bernoulli beam reveal that architectural improvements alone are insufficient: accurate solutions require the combination of PI-SUPNs, FP64 precision, and curvature-aware optimization. Additionally, Allen-Cahn experiments show that PI-SUPNs achieve lower solution and derivative errors at reduced computational cost, with more favorable loss landscapes than competing architectures. We also establish quasi-local approximation properties and spline-based convergence bounds for SUPNs. Our results show that shallow network architectures are an important mechanism for improving physics-informed trainability, but accurate solutions to the most challenging PDEs can still require FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization.
authors: Zachary Morrow, Yucheng Fu, Pratanu Roy

title: Beyond Gaussian Calibration: Local Inference in Decentralized SGD
abstract: Decentralized SGD minimizes a common objective by local gradient steps and neighbor averaging. Its statistical theory mostly concerns network averages, yet clients act on their own iterates, and one-sided decisions such as alarms use one tail of the local error. We show that a client's constant-step endpoint can have nearly nominal Gaussian coverage while both tails are badly miscalibrated. An exact noise-filter representation explains why: a quantity computable from the graph and stepsize decides whether the endpoint is asymptotically Gaussian, and when the number of clients outgrows the inverse stepsize on networks with summable return probabilities, such as lazy tori of dimension at least three and expanders, a few recent noise terms at nearby clients keep a fixed share of local variance. On these tori the limit is a non-Gaussian local field plus an independent Gaussian consensus term, and no reference distribution built from finitely many noise moments, including Edgeworth and Cornish--Fisher corrections, is calibrated at all levels uniformly over noise laws. We propose a hybrid reference that resamples the influential noise terms from their empirical law and replaces the rest by a Gaussian; its non-asymptotic coverage bound allows noise laws and curvature estimated from fresh gradients or the client's trajectory, and extends to nonlinear vector objectives. In full-network simulations it restores tail balance at essentially unchanged interval length, also under rare large shocks that break Cornish--Fisher intervals; gains vanish, as predicted, when consensus dominates.
authors: Xiaoli Li, Qianqian Lei, Wei Biao Wu

title: Directional Bias in Quantile SGD and Score-Inversion Inference under Dependence
abstract: Quantile stochastic gradient descent (SGD) tracks a quantile by comparing each observation with an adaptive threshold, and closely related updates calibrate online conformal sets and drive quantile temporal-difference learning. Their inputs are serially dependent, yet existing guarantees largely assume independence. We show that dependence creates a directional bias that score autocovariances cannot detect: reversing a stationary stream leaves every score autocovariance unchanged but can change the leading bias threefold. For finite memory and decreasing stepsizes, the bias splits into lag-specific interactions between the threshold and the current observation and a curvature term; delaying the threshold removes the interactions one lag at a time while keeping every observation and the leading variance. At stepsizes near $t^{-1/2}$, as used for online inference, the bias is comparable to the standard error and makes an SGD-based interval miss mostly on one side. Testing fixed candidates instead keeps the score centered, so calibration depends only on score autocovariances. Extending local-dependence self-normalized approximations to the implemented acceptance hull, we show that inverting these tests gives a density-free, moment-free interval for the population quantile with $O(n^{-1/2})$ coverage error for a fixed sufficient lag window, a rate that is sharp for this interval, and a guarantee for data-selected windows; an exact scan takes $O(n\log n)$ time. Experiments confirm the lag-by-lag predictions and show calibration competitive with block bootstrap at lower cost.
authors: Xiaoli Li, Qianqian Lei, Wei Biao Wu

title: Real-time event-level zero-shot learning at 150 ns: towards a foundation model for particle physics experiment triggering
abstract: The hardware-based Level-1 triggers of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) experiments select collisions with algorithms designed for one signature each, acting on a coarse, low-latency view of every event. We present a learned event embedding for several trigger tasks and evaluate its transfer to processes absent from training. Using paired offline and Level-1 views of the same simulated collisions, we train an offline transformer with a supervised metric loss and distil it, event by event, into a quantised Level-1 transformer whose bit widths are learned under a fixed resource budget. Trained on 25 Standard Model processes, the embedding places 28 held-out processes next to their physical relatives. A nearest-neighbour selection against background collisions, which never enter encoder training, rejects 99% of them. It retains a median of 90% of seen and 96% of unseen Standard Model events and 88% of a set of 52 beyond-the-Standard-Model benchmark samples, the best-performing score across the three groups among the baselines evaluated on the same events. A second gate against the seen processes isolates high-mass dilepton signals into label-free clusters, and long-lived signals too when displaced-track information is available. With 7512 parameters and an FPGA latency of 147 ns, the encoder uses one event representation, learned once, to derive several selections, opening the door to a foundation model for the LHC's hardware-based triggers.
authors: Leo Rozanov, Lauri Laatu, Benedikt Maier

title: Coupling-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Co-Evolving Graph Games
abstract: Building hydrogen station networks, electric vehicle charging grids, or vaccine distribution systems requires coordinating two separately operated graphs, demand-side facilities and the supply-side networks they depend on, where each operator's payoff depends on the other's choices. We formalize this as the Co-Evolving Graph Game (CEGG), a setting that sits between facility location, interdependent-network analysis, and graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) but is not jointly addressed by any of them. We propose Cross-Graph Attention with Policy Mirror Descent (CGA-PMD), pairing cross-graph attention, which lets each agent read only the partner-graph nodes structurally coupled to its own, with a policy mirror descent update for stable training. Across three reward domains and a range of practical network scales, we find that the structure of the coupling selects which method wins: at small scale most methods are competitive, but as scale grows or coupling becomes irregular, CGA-PMD is the one method that stays reliable: it attains the highest success count on each of five real city networks, while own-only, unmasked-attention, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based variants degrade in distinct ways. Our theoretical analysis addresses the optimizer side: the Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularized update admits an iteration-uniform cumulative drift bound, whereas the clip update admits no such bound on the iterations where the clip does not bind. The implementation is available at https://github.com/Mina-Kim-Github/cegg-cga-pmd.
authors: Mina Kim, Guanghui Lan, Benoit Montreuil

title: Toward Adversarially Robust World Models
abstract: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.
authors: Ethan Rathbun, Jonathan Nöther, Christopher Amato

title: Which Loans, Not How Many: Exactly Level-Invariant, Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Deployed Risk Models
abstract: A refinancing wave can change the number of mortgage prepayments without changing the relationship between scores and prepayment. In a logistic model, conditioning on the monthly count removes the intercept from the likelihood of which loans prepay. Our fixed-start slope product tests a lower bound on the calibration slope. At threshold 20 its probability of ever crossing under the null is at most 5%. The restarted level sum tracks departures from intercept tolerance. A confidence sequence estimates a constant slope, and the restart-intersection rule detects changes in that slope. A continuous mixture avoids the off-grid width floor of a discrete prior. On Freddie Mac loans, fixed-slope resampling reproduces 78% of maintained-model monthly AUC variance in development and 70% in the holdout (95% intervals 57-100% and 48-100%). From fresh holdout starts, the restarted level sum crosses on both paths, and the fixed-start slope product stays below threshold on both. The restart-intersection rule signals a downward change for the frozen model in April 2018 and an upward change for the maintained model in a supplementary run in August 2019.
authors: Xin Xu

title: TabK: Amortized Bayesian Estimation of the Number of Clusters in Tabular Data
abstract: Estimating the number of clusters, $k$, is a fundamental prerequisite for most clustering algorithms. Traditionally, this estimation has relied on computationally expensive grid searches over internal cluster validity indices (CVIs) or adaptive clustering algorithms, both constrained by specific statistical assumptions. We introduce TabK, a zero-shot, permutation-invariant transformer architecture that frames the estimation of $k$ as an amortized Bayesian inference problem for tabular data. TabK leverages a novel Quantile Feature Encoder (QFE) to extract position-free, content-derived representations from empirical marginal distributions. By learning a generalized structural bias over a diverse synthetic prior, TabK estimates the number of clusters in a single forward pass per ensemble member. Evaluated across 50 diverse real-world benchmarks, TabK outperforms all competing methods, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) value of 1.04 compared to 2.14 for the closest competitor. TabK also achieves the lowest average inference time, producing estimates in less than one second on average and running $2\times$ faster than TabClustPFN and $30\times$ faster than traditional CVIs such as Silhouette and Calinski-Harabasz. Code is available at https://github.com/mrbakhtyari/TabK.
authors: Mohammadreza Bakhtyari, Bogdan Mazoure, Renato Cordeiro de Amorim

title: AV-FLARE: Feature-Level Reliability Estimation for Multimodal Emotion Recognition
abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition (MMER) systems typically rely on learned feature representations and attention mechanisms that implicitly weight information across time and modalities. However, these mechanisms do not explicitly incorporate input reliability, despite the presence of noise in audio, occlusions in visual data, and the sparse and event-driven nature of affective cues. We propose AV-FLARE, a framework that explicitly estimates fine-grained reliability scores across both temporal and feature dimensions prior to temporal modeling and uses them to modulate feature representations. Reliability is computed using two complementary components: (i) a supervised network trained jointly with the classification objective, and (ii) an unsupervised Gaussian Mixture Model that models global feature distributions. These signals are combined to provide both task-driven and distribution-aware reliability estimates. To integrate modalities, we introduce a hierarchical cross-modal attention mechanism in which textual features are used to guide audio-visual fusion as a semantic reference modality. Experiments on the IEMOCAP dataset show that AV-FLARE improves over a no-reliability baseline, achieving 90.81\% accuracy and 81.69\% F1-score, corresponding to gains of +4.41% and +8.56%, respectively. These results suggest that incorporating explicit input reliability estimation may improve robustness in multimodal emotion recognition under the evaluated setting.
authors: Ines Jemmali, Alaa Nfissi, Wassim Bouachir

title: Click and Count: Multimodal Prototype Adaptation for Class-Agnostic Object Counting
abstract: We propose a multimodal, class-agnostic, density-based object counting framework that specifies the object of interest through visual exemplars, a text description, or both, within a single iterative refinement pipeline. Existing counters typically fall into two groups: methods that fuse two modalities, a hand-drawn bounding box and a text description, to specify the target object, and single-modality methods that rely on either a box exemplar or text alone. A few recent methods replace the box with a point or click. We expand a single click into a precise object mask via a frozen visual-prompt segmentation model, feeding an iterative prototype-refinement process that also fuses a text description at every refinement step. We make two contributions: first, a click-derived exemplar extraction module that removes the bounding-box requirement of prior exemplar-based counters; second, a per-step text-fusion mechanism that combines visual and textual prompts throughout refinement. Combined with text guidance, our model achieves state-of-the-art counting accuracy, outperforming prior click-based counting methods across all metrics and surpassing the box-exemplar base architecture in mean absolute error. The code is available at github.com/ameniifi/Click-and-Count.
authors: Amani Aifi, Wassim Bouachir, Ahmed Zgaren

title: An LLM-Assisted Multi-Objective AutoML Framework for Efficient Network Intrusion Detection
abstract: Conventional Machine Learning (ML)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) require manual design, optimize only detection performance, and neglect inference latency and model size, which are critical for resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) and Electric Vehicle Charging System (EVCS) deployments. Automated ML (AutoML) reduces manual effort but explores broad search spaces inefficiently. Meanwhile, Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) methods lack guided search initialization, leading to long search times. This paper proposes a Large Language Model-Assisted Multi-Objective Automated ML (LLM-MOO-AutoML) framework for efficient intrusion detection. A local Llama 3.1 8B model analyzes a compact dataset profile and generates a bounded, validated policy for automated data balancing (AutoDP) and feature engineering (AutoFE). This policy narrows the search space for Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III (NSGA-III), which jointly optimizes the LightGBM feature-selection threshold and key hyperparameters across three objectives: maximizing weighted F1-score, minimizing 99th-percentile (P99) inference latency ratio, and minimizing model size ratio. Experiments on CICIDS2017, IoTID20, and CICEVSE2024 demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves the highest weighted F1-scores on CICIDS2017 (99.788%), IoTID20 (99.778%), and CICEVSE2024 (99.989%), with feature sets reduced to as few as 10 features, P99 latency as low as 0.00038 ms, and model size as small as 0.1073 MB. The LLM-guided configuration reduced NSGA-III search time relative to unconstrained multi-objective search on all datasets at the largest trial budget and in most comparisons at smaller budgets, indicating that dataset-aware search-space reduction supports efficient, deployment-aware intrusion detection.
authors: Ailin Barzegar, Khalil El-Khatib, Li Yang

title: Benchmarking EEG feature families for ADHD research in children and adolescents: performance and explainability across attention tasks
abstract: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder varies in presentation. Diagnosis requires clinical and developmental assessment. Reproducible electroencephalography measures may complement clinical and behavioural characterisation, but differing feature definitions and evaluation methods hinder comparison. We compared seven feature families and four combinations across attention tasks and assessed the stability of held-out explanations. Two serious games yielded four overlapping attention-task cohorts of 123-140 participants each. Repeated nested participant-held-out evaluation assessed recruitment-group discrimination. Exploratory paired participant-cluster bootstrap tests corrected for multiplicity in two separate families: 72 individual-task contrasts and 18 fusion contrasts. For eight configurations selected after inspecting predictive results, we explained held-out native probabilities before calibration. In the strongest task context, the highest configuration mean AUROC over three repetitions was 0.773, with a fixed-prediction 95% interval of 0.692-0.854 unadjusted for selecting the maximum. Precision, sensitivity and specificity were 0.740, 0.556 and 0.861. In that task, the paired AUROC difference for connectivity minus spectral features averaged +0.2083 across six classifiers and the common 8 s and 16 s durations, with pointwise 95% CI 0.1076-0.3072 and adjusted p = 0.0036. F4-AF4 beta-band coherence led repetition-level attribution summaries in five selected procedures and was selected in every fit. Other contexts showed weaker discrimination and less consistent retention of leading scientific inputs. No general classifier winner emerged. Connectivity and its recurring coherence input warrant independent replication, but do not justify a universal feature recommendation. These exploratory findings do not establish causal task effects, disease mechanisms or diagnostic validity.
authors: Javier Sanchis, Jorge García-Carrasco, Álvaro Navarro

title: Intervention-Robust VLA: Diverse Demonstrations for Robot Deployment with Safety Filters
abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have shown strong potential for learning complex robotic behaviors from demonstrations. However, learning safe behavior directly from data requires extensive coverage of safety-critical situations, which is often impractical in real-world settings. Test-time safety filters provide an alternative by correcting unsafe actions during deployment, but these interventions can drive the robot into states poorly covered by the training data, thereby degrading task performance. We introduce InteR-VLA, an intervention-robust framework for VLAs that leverages diverse task-completing demonstrations to broaden task-relevant state coverage and maintain competence under safety interventions. By better aligning the training distribution with safety-filtered deployment under the same data budget, our approach mitigates intervention-induced distribution shift while preserving task performance. Real-world experiments across in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings show that InteR-VLA maintains safety, increases Safe Success Rate up to 90% from 0% for nominal policies, and consistently outperforms nominal-data training on both evaluated VLAs.
authors: Tzu-Yuan Huang, Shao-Hsuan Chang, Dai-Jie Wu

title: Scalable Beckmann Maps Improve One-step Generation
abstract: Beckmann Transport Models (BTM) learn one-step generative maps end-to-end from data, without a teacher, a distillation stage, or pretrained features. We introduce Scalable Beckmann Maps (SBM), which bring to BTM the two ingredients behind the quality of modern multistep generators: classifier-free guidance (CFG) and a training recipe that scales, while keeping sampling at a single network evaluation. CFG combines conditional and unconditional velocity or score predictions, which a Beckmann map does not have. Our guidance rests on one observation: the BTM current is a positive multiple of an autonomous denoising field, to which CFG applies as it does to a velocity. With exact denoisers this gives guided BTM. In practice we substitute the map's own conditional and null predictions for the denoisers, which requires no additional network and introduces a bias that we characterize. We show that the guided update is consistent with a guided conservation equation, and that guidance can move the boundaries between basins, sending more noise to the modes a condition favors. Trained from scratch in the latent of a representation autoencoder, SBM reaches a one-step FID of 1.6 on ImageNet 256x256 without a teacher or a feature loss, outperforming the Improved-MeanFlow baseline with 3.2x fewer FLOPs. In text-to-image generation it reaches a GenEval score of 0.86 with one network evaluation. As a world model, where we train without guidance, the recipe alone outperforms DriftWorld on all five metrics of two robot-manipulation benchmarks, with 1.9-2.8x less training compute and no pretrained auxiliary feature encoder.
authors: Ulrik Unneberg, Shiyi Wang, Lee Cheuk-Kit

title: Neural Fidelity Calibration for Informative Sim-to-Real Adaptation
abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can transfer agile robot skills from simulation to the real world, but closing the sim-to-real gap by domain randomization requires expert physics knowledge, and simulator calibration from real data typically targets a few hand-picked parameters. Even then, simulators miss real-world effects, and environments reconstructed from onboard perception inherit sensing errors that limit policy improvement. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), which uses conditional flow matching to calibrate simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity domains online during deployment. Residual fidelity captures sim-to-real dynamics discrepancies and perception-induced environment uncertainty. NFC operates in a latent space so that realistic environments can be sampled from the inferred posterior for real-to-sim policy fine-tuning. The framework is informative: the pretrained policy is fine-tuned only when an anomaly is detected, sequential NFC seeds its proposal from the simulation-pretrained estimator, and a hallucination policy modulates posterior uncertainty following optimism in the face of uncertainty. NFC attains the most accurate posteriors among established simulation-based inference methods on five robots with up to 39 physical parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain. On a wheeled robot with a broken wheel axle deployed on snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC raises success on rough terrain from 26% to 70% and reduces orientation jerk by 88%. Code and videos will be released upon publication.
authors: Youwei Yu, Lantao Liu

title: What Do Differentiable Rule Learners Need? FLARE: Fuzzy Rules with Additive Evidence
abstract: Rule learners are used where transparency and accountability are required, because they give practitioners patterns they can read. Learning rules is a discrete problem, so neurosymbolic pipelines that use rules as explanations rely on relaxations such as the straight-through estimator. However, these differentiable rule learners often lag behind both classical rule learners and black-box classifiers in terms of performance. We study which parts of a rule-based classifier affect performance, and how well gradient-based training learns each of them. We found that most of the performance comes from how the rules are weighted: random rules with learned weights are already more accurate than every published differentiable rule learner we tested. Based on our results, we propose FLARE (Fuzzy Learned-Antecedent Rule Evidence), a differentiable rule learner that learns simple rules that combine to make the final decision. We also propose a learned encoding for variables with thousands of categories. We test FLARE on tabular data, using 42 datasets of OpenML-CC18 and the 38 classification tasks of TabArena. On CC18, FLARE exceeds the compared rule learners by 7.69 to 12.38 macro-F1 points and performs comparably to random forests, while remaining 1.00 to 1.11 points below tuned gradient-boosted trees. On TabArena it ranks at the same level as random forests and ahead of the other rule learners. As the concept-to-label head of a concept bottleneck model, FLARE is the best rule-based head in five of six settings. On graphs, it is competitive on PubMed and EMOGI but falls behind graph neural networks on Cora and Citeseer. Our code is available at https://github.com/Fuminides/FLARE
authors: Javier Fumanal-Idocin, Javier Andreu-Perez

title: SONATI: Spatio-temporal ocean neighbourhood asymmetric transformer for imputation of sparse, tabular data with uncertainty
abstract: Missing value imputation is often a prerequisite for downstream analyses. In oceanography, observational data are frequently structured in a tabular manner, highly sparse and exhibit spatio-temporal structures that classical imputers such as k-nearest neighbours or MissForest are not suited to exploit. We present the Spatio-temporal Ocean Neighbourhood Asymmetric Transformer for Imputation (SONATI), a masked, factorised time-space transformer operating on pre-computed, local time and space neighbourhoods, which reduces computational complexity compared to global attention. SONATI is designed to work with tabular data and is thus in principle able to work on both gridded and unstructured data, though evaluation here was performed on gridded North Atlantic data only. It provides aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties through a negative log-likelihood loss and multiple forward passes with Monte Carlo dropout. Systematic ablations on attention type and masking strategies guided the final architecture design. The results showed that SONATI outperformed classical and transformer-based methods by at least 12.5% in terms of root mean squared error (RMSE) on a large observational oceanographic dataset with key biogeochemical and physical parameters in the North Atlantic (potential temperature, salinity, oxygen, nitrate, silicate and phosphate). Attention type and masking strategy strongly affected imputation accuracy and smoothness of the produced oceanographic fields. Best results were achieved by factorised time-space attention and combined geographic and per-sample masking. The combined masking strategy reduced the imputation error by 14.3% compared to per-sample masking only. Uncertainties were moderately well calibrated (miscalibration area at observed locations $0.074\pm0.012$) and moderately correlated with the imputation error.
authors: Yvonne Jenniges, Boris Peter Koch, Maike Sonnewald

title: Failure Modes and Data-Efficient Remedies for Transformer-Based Prediction of Viscoplastic Flows
abstract: Fast and accurate prediction of viscoplastic flows remains a challenge in computational rheology due to yield surfaces, discontinuous gradients, and strongly nonlinear transitions between yielded and unyielded regions. Transformer-based neural operators such as RheOFormer have recently shown strong potential for surrogate modeling of non-Newtonian flows. However, their applicability to viscoplastic systems and their efficacy in recovering realistic flows remain poorly understood. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of RheOFormer applied to steady Bingham channel flow. By isolating the problem to a simple geometry and constitutive model, we examine how dataset structure, numerical value range, and input representation govern the model's ability to interpolate and extrapolate within the parameter space. The data regimes in which RheOFormer remains accurate and those in which errors emerge are identified, particularly for plug-dominated flows and for conditions outside the velocity scales or flow structures represented during training. Upon identifying these failure modes, targeted enhancements to the input representation and loss formulation are introduced to better predict low-gradient plug regions. Logarithmic velocity representations and gradient-aware loss formulations substantially improve accuracy in challenging regimes where the baseline formulation fails. In addition, extrapolation errors are reduced by augmenting the training set with only a few strategically selected cases spanning the missing physical regimes. Finally, a single partially developed snapshot suffices for an accurate steady-state prediction, and the model outperforms simply copying its input throughout flow development. These results highlight the importance of appropriate field representation and parameter-space coverage for data-efficient neural-operator prediction of viscoplastic flows.
authors: Maedeh Saberi, Hugo Franca, Maziyar Jalaal

title: FoGConcept: Identifying Interpretable Movement Concepts for Freezing-of-Gait Detection from Multi-Scale IMU Signals
abstract: Freezing of gait (FoG) is a disabling motor symptom of Parkinson's disease, characterized by an episodic inability to initiate or sustain effective stepping. Current inertial measurement unit (IMU)-based models can detect FoG accurately, but they fail to explain their predictions in terms of human-understandable movement concepts. A major contribution of this work is to identify nine human-understandable movement concepts encoded by a multi-scale FoG model, including gait initiation, rhythmic bilateral gait, trembling in place, shuffling steps, and pivot turns. These concepts recur across subjects, are functionally linked to the model's FoG decisions, and exhibit emergent specialization across short and long temporal contexts. Repeating the concept-discovery procedure on a new FoG dataset, wider temporal contexts, and a deeper backbone recovers the same comparatively stable set of movement concepts. Accordingly, we propose FoGConcept, a mechanism-based interpretability framework for learning movement concepts from multi-scale IMU signals. Domain experts independently recognize 88.9% of the identified concepts, while the proposed model achieves an F1 score of 94.2% for FoG detection. Our findings show that accurate FoG detection can be understood through human-recognizable movement patterns, providing new insight into what a detection model learns to distinguish FoG from non-FoG movement.
authors: Chuntian Chi, John Clapham, GinaMari Blackwell

title: Mitigating large circuits with a learned small-circuit mitigator
abstract: Learning-based quantum error mitigation infers noise-free results from noisy measurement data. However, exact training labels become prohibitively expensive to compute as circuits grow, and the generalization capability of a trained model to infer accurate results on circuits of depths and sizes it was not trained on poses a challenge. We show that circuit cutting allows such a model to be reused on circuits larger than those it was trained on. We benchmark this approach against zero-noise extrapolation, Clifford data regression, and probabilistic error cancellation on simulated circuits several times wider and deeper than the training circuits. On random-circuit chains, the fragment-wise mitigator removes most of the reconstructed error. For a holographic Ising-chain eigensolver under a fixed shot budget, it recovers most of the noise-induced energy error, close to 90\% or more, and outperforms Clifford data regression and probabilistic error cancellation. Since the mitigator is trained once and needs no additional circuits or noise amplification at inference, its cost is paid up front rather than for every new circuit. The approach is also modular. Any improvement to the small-circuit mitigator, such as retraining on larger fragments or on device-specific noise, carries over directly to every circuit that can be cut into such fragments. Our proposal thus offers a practical route to bringing learned error mitigation to quantum computations far beyond the reach of exact training labels, provided they can be partitioned with a moderate number of cuts.
authors: Thi Ha Kyaw, Pablo Díez-Valle, Gaurav Saxena

title: The Cross-Context Threshold Test: Detecting Discrimination Under Environmental Shifts
abstract: We study how threshold tests for detecting discrimination under environmental shifts, focusing on the Veil-of-Darkness (VoD) setting where visibility changes between daylight and darkness. We show that standard threshold tests, when applied separately to daylight and darkness data, violate key assumptions: risk distributions drift across contexts and thresholds fluctuate arbitrarily. We propose a cross-context threshold test that enforces distributional invariance and monotonic threshold decay. Using New York City stop-and-frisk data and synthetic experiments, we demonstrate that this model yields more reliable thresholds, improves bias detection, and aligns with the counterfactual logic of the VoD test. Our framework generalizes to fairness auditing whenever environmental context influences decisions.
authors: Jun Yuan, Xinyue Ye

title: Variable Importance Recovery in Tabular Foundation Models: A Simulation Study
abstract: In machine learning, identifying which variables contribute predictive information can be as important as predictive accuracy. Tabular foundation models have matched or exceeded the predictive performance of tuned gradient boosting trees on many small- and medium-sized tabular datasets. Yet their ability to recover population-level variable importance has received little attention. We design and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation study to compare variable importance recovery across tabular foundation models and established machine learning baselines. Our framework distinguishes multiple population estimands, pairs each one with an aligned model-agnostic importance estimator, and evaluates recovery in terms of ranking, support, and relative magnitude. Our results show that tabular foundation models are generally competitive with established machine-learning baselines in recovering population variable importance, and often more accurate. We thus extend the evidence for their capabilities to a previously underexamined dimension, further strengthening their appeal.
authors: Vasil Yasenov, Nicholas Adams-Cohen

title: Learning the Projection onto the Data Support: Distribution Learning that Avoids Memorization
abstract: We introduce a framework for learning distributions supported on manifolds based on estimating the nearest-point projection onto the data support. Specifically, we define an objective functional over a class of functions whose minimizer recovers this projection. The proposed framework automatically adapts to the intrinsic dimension and allows for data supported on unions of manifolds with varying dimensions. The resulting objective can be optimized using standard neural network architectures. We present population-level results establishing recovery of the manifold projection and prove finite-sample Wasserstein generalization bounds. Furthermore, we validate the approach empirically across a range of settings. In contrast to widely used generative models such as diffusion models, whose objectives can be minimized by memorizing training samples, our formulation excludes such behavior. We also introduce a direct memorization metric to verify that the learned projection generates new samples rather than reproducing the training set.
authors: Lin Chen, Dejan Slepčev

title: Feedback Shortcut: Speculative Decoding for Latent Feedback Transformers
abstract: Feeding each position's top-layer hidden state back into the next position's input improves Transformer performance. However, this feedback breaks speculative decoding, since verifying a drafted token requires the top-layer state from its preceding position, which forces the draft to rely on an approximate stand-in. Training the model to adapt to this stand-in can lower the exact-decoding performance ceiling, while using it at inference time further introduces approximation error. We propose Feedback Shortcut to address both bottlenecks. First, state alignment trains a lightweight projection from multi-token prediction head states to stand-ins, leaving base model training untouched. Second, pipelined correction re-evaluates each draft using its predecessor's newly computed state, a much closer proxy to true feedback. Running this correction inside the verification pass of subsequent drafts improves accuracy with zero extra calls. Across 135M and 780M scales, Feedback Shortcut stays within $10^{-4}$ bits per byte of the exact-decoding ceiling on Paloma and accelerates decoding by 2.4-2.8x with about 2% more training compute than the latent feedback Transformer. At large batch sizes, skipping correction still preserves Transformer speed and over 80% of latent feedback's gains.
authors: Benhao Huang, Xuezhe Ma, Hector Liu

title: A Methodologically Rigorous Benchmark of Linear Regression,RNN, and LSTM for S&P 500 Forecasting:Identifying Sources of Performance Inflation in Financial DeepLearning
abstract: This study examines one-day-ahead forecasting of the S&P 500 closing level using a 2006-2025 dataset that includes fundamental price data, macroeconomic indicators, and engineered technical features. We benchmark three model families, namely linear regression, vanilla recurrent neural networks (RNN), and long short-term memory networks (LSTM), within a unified preprocessing and chronological evaluation pipeline. A central contribution of this work is a methodological audit of common practices in the deep-learning-for-stock-prediction literature. We identify three sources of result inflation that frequently appear in published methodologies: wavelet-denoised evaluation targets, the absence of a naive persistence baseline, and best-of-N replicate reporting. We then re-evaluate all model families under a corrected protocol that controls for each. Performance is reported using root mean squared error, mean absolute percentage error, and the Pearson correlation coefficient, averaged across N = 30 independent replicates per configuration. We compare models on accuracy, stability across replicates, and architectural depth sensitivity, using the naive persistence forecast (predicting today's close as tomorrow's close) as a primary baseline against which all candidate models must demonstrate improvement.
authors: Hari Sitaula, Joseph Opitz

title: On the Complete Feature Set for ADHD Classification in Children and Adolescents Based on EEG Signals
abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity and impulse control. Electroencephalography (EEG) records brain activity as children and adolescents perform cognitive tasks. However, comparing features derived from these recordings requires consistent signal preparation, shared analysis windows and documented quality decisions. We curated 669 existing BALLADEER recordings from 156 participants across five task conditions so that researchers can compare seven EEG feature families on the same time intervals for each participant and task. The dataset links continuous signals to precomputed measurements from 115 feature definitions or templates and records the quality decisions made for each recording. Analyses must still account for repeated measurements within participants, residual artefacts and differences between acquisition systems. Technical validation covered signal integrity, numerical checks on feature estimators and completeness of the released files. In every task, the median proportion of recording time retained after preprocessing was 100%. To illustrate reuse, we report saved participant-held-out evaluations comparing XGBoost using all seven families on eight-second windows with a predictor based only on recruitment-group prevalence in the training fold. Recruitment-group discrimination was stronger in Robots than in the three Slackline conditions. These descriptive results from overlapping cohorts do not establish diagnostic validity. The dataset, curation software and aggregate results for the predictive example are publicly available.
authors: Javier Sanchis, Álvaro Navarro, Jorge García-Carrasco

title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization
abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. The method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is then used for HPO with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that RPC substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across decision tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, HPO-stage speedups range from approximately 1.14x to 8.80x, while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations excluded from coreset construction, RPC achieves higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014). These results show that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. The one-time construction cost can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs.
authors: Mamoona Tasadduq, Maryam Bashir

title: Topology Hub Optimal Transport: Eliminating Long Context Dilution at Flash Speed
abstract: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($α=0$) and 98.83% at $α=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $α=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $α=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. Zero-shot WikiText-103 multi-needle retrieval hits 100.00% (128/128 queries at $L=65\mathrm{K}$) vs. 0.78% for short-trained RoPE FlashAttention, and compact 4-layer WikiText-4K runs show modest causal and masked LM gains.
authors: Dylan Forde

title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Agnostic PAC Learning for Partial Concept Classes
abstract: Let $\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1,\star\}^{\mathcal X}$ be a partial concept class of finite VC dimension $d$. We construct a deterministic agnostic PAC learner that, for every $\varepsilon,δ\in(0,1)$, uses $O((d+\log(1/δ))/\varepsilon^2)$ i.i.d. examples from an arbitrary distribution $\mathcal D$ over $\mathcal X\times\{-1,+1\}$ and returns a total concept $\hat h:\mathcal X\to\{-1,+1\}$ satisfying $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(\hat h)\leq \min_{h\in\mathcal H}\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)+\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-δ$, where $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)=\mathbb P_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal D}[h(x)\neq y]$. This establishes the optimal sample complexity, matching the lower bound of Alon et al. (FOCS 2021).
authors: Liang-Yu Zou

title: Hidden Clues in WM-811K: Uncovering the Spatial Signals Behind Wafer Map Prediction
abstract: WM-811K (also known as LSWMD) is a wafer map dataset first made publicly available in a 2015 paper by Wu et al. Convolutional neural networks have been used to achieve high classification accuracy on this dataset, yet it's not easy to decipher which features of the dataset are driving that performance. This study attempts to answer this specifically for WM-811K: how much of the predictive performance results from the wafer layout, the count of failed dies, their distance from the center and their exact 2-D location. After analyzing duplicate wafer maps, removing same wafer maps with conflicting labels and ensuring that the same manufacturing lot or exact same map doesn't appear in training, validation and test data, we were left with 25,513 defect-labeled wafer maps from eight classes. We then constructed four variations of each wafer map. The Original was the actual wafer map present in the dataset. The Layout-only kept only the layout of the non-background dies. The Global-shuffle kept the count of failed dies while shuffling them around. The Radial-shuffle randomized the locations of failed dies only in their radial bin, which was chosen out of 8 radial bins based on distance from the center. The data split, preprocessing and CNN architecture remained the same for all four of them. Macro-F1 progressed like this: 0.3829 (Layout-only), 0.5803 (Global-shuffle), 0.7439 (Radial-shuffle) and 0.8563 (Original). These results show that WM-811K contains useful information at several levels: wafer layout, number of failures, distribution of failed dies in a given radius, and exact 2-D locations of the failed dies. Therefore, high classification performance on this benchmark does not come only from learning the exact defect configuration.
authors: Kabir Tolani

title: Communication-Efficient Federated Learning of Latent Patient Representations from Multi-Institutional EHRs
abstract: Electronic health records (EHRs) contain rich health information for uncovering latent patient representations and clinically meaningful subgroups. Learning from EHR data across institutions is valuable because representations learned at a single site may reflect local data patterns and lack generalizability, yet pooling patient-level records across institutions is often impractical because of privacy constraints and communication costs. We propose a communication-efficient, non-iterative federated spectral method for learning shared latent representation components from multi-institutional EHRs, in which each institution shares aggregate marginal frequencies and a low-rank spectral summary while keeping patient-level records local. A central server aggregates these summaries with the pooled marginal frequencies to recover both the shared low-rank structure and the canonical row-normalization direction required for interpretable representation recovery. We prove row-wise recovery guarantees and error bounds, with a leading federated variance term matching a corresponding lower bound under explicit regularity conditions. Simulations show that our method closely matches pooled analysis in estimating latent representation components, improves as more sites contribute summaries, and outperforms single-site and existing federated benchmarks across a range of data settings. Applied to real-world multi-facility EHR data for stroke patients, the method learns interpretable patient representations that highlight clinically distinct subgroups and could help inform subgroup-specific care.
authors: Zhiyu Yan, Shiao Liu, Rahul Mahajan

title: FairITR: Fairness-Aware Learning of Multicategory Individualized Treatment Rules
abstract: Individualized treatment rules (ITRs) recommend treatment decisions based on individual characteristics and can improve treatment outcomes beyond traditional one-size-fits-all strategies. However, similar to other commonly used algorithmic decision-making methods, ITRs without considering model fairness may result in unfair decisions across groups defined by sensitive attributes, such as race or gender. Although extensive methods have been developed for ITR estimation, most focus solely on optimizing treatment outcomes, while research on fairness-aware ITRs remains limited. Moreover, the practical scenario of multicategory treatments is rarely considered in existing fair ITR studies. To address these gaps, we introduce a fairness notion for multicategory ITRs that requires treatment decisions to be independent of sensitive attributes, and then formulate the corresponding problem of estimating fair ITRs. To solve this problem, we further propose FairITR, a fairness-aware learning framework that jointly optimizes treatment outcomes and fairness. FairITR builds on angle-based classification for multicategory ITR learning and integrates adversarial learning with covariance-based regularization to mitigate unfairness in treatment decisions. A theoretical justification for the fairness properties induced by the adversarial debiasing mechanism is also provided. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that FairITR substantially reduces unfairness in ITRs while maintaining competitive treatment values relative to existing baselines.
authors: Zeyu Chen, Wei Qian, Bintong Chen

title: Renormalized Entropy from Symmetries: Simplicity Bias and Neural Heat Death
abstract: Neural networks have parameter symmetries: parameter transformations that do not affect the represented function. How do these symmetries affect the functions that neural networks ultimately learn? We study the implicit bias arising from these symmetries by calculating the equilibrium distribution over represented functions under Langevin dynamics with Gaussian regularization. To isolate the effect of symmetries on this distribution, we study the limit in which the strength of the regularization is taken to zero. In certain cases, we show that the zero-regularization and infinite-time limits commute. In the low temperature limit, we recover known effective regularizations. At positive temperature, a renormalization procedure allows us to derive a novel entropy which predicts symmetry-induced preference for certain functions. For linear networks, we obtain explicit entropy terms that favor singular and low-rank functions. For networks with homogeneous activations, we find entropy terms that favor inactive neurons, which can lead to neural "heat death" in which equilibrium mass concentrates on networks with vanishing output. We interpret these results through the neural tangent kernel, as a simplicity bias selecting for functions that vary slowly under variations in the parameters.
authors: Vasco Portilheiro, Samuel Liebana, Andrew Saxe

title: From Gist to Verbatim: The Controllable Path of One Image Through a Diffusion Prior
abstract: Modern generative models are typically studied for their ability to generalize, while memorization is treated as a failure mode. We invert this perspective and ask how a generative model can recall a single datum. We frame memorization as a control problem: a learned conditioning signal steers a frozen diffusion model toward a target image, and we follow the formation of this memory throughout training. Before converging to exact reproduction (verbatim), memory passes through a regime of abstraction: samples preserve the target's semantic content (gist) while remaining diverse in appearance, leaving predictable detail to the generative prior. This semantic organization emerges despite the absence of labels, captions, or any explicit semantic objective. In the abstraction regime, the learned memory approaches ordinary text conditioning and supports editing, one-shot recognition, and retrieval more effectively than in the near-perfect reconstruction regime. These results suggest that memorization can serve as a probe of the relevance structure encoded by a generative model: what must be stored about a datum, what can be reconstructed from prior knowledge, and how learned memories interpolate between reconstructive recall and literal data storage.
authors: Luca Saglietti, Luca Giammanco, Marc Mezard

title: Anchors That Move Without Collapsing: Exclusive-Region Anchor Routing for Vision Transformers
abstract: Anchor tokens let a vision transformer exchange global information through a few summaries, but nothing forces different anchors to summarise different things. On one shared backbone we show that a Perceiver-style pathway and an AnchorFormer pathway collapse to a single summary, the latter despite its mass normalisation (pooling-map similarity 0.99), while other soft pathways, including Representative Attention, stay partly redundant (0.59-0.79). These results concern the routing modules inside our block, not the full published models. An exclusive partition of the patch grid cannot collapse by construction, and matched component by component it is 2.4-3.6 points more accurate than Representative Attention on CIFAR-100. We then propose focus anchors, which place most anchors at the peaks of a learned importance map while all anchors keep one exclusive Voronoi partition. Focus anchors beat a fixed partition on a cluttered canvas (+1.5 points, 95% CI [0.5, 2.6]) but not on full-HD traffic-sign recognition. There, both variants match dense attention with local windows at about a fifth of its FLOPs, and the fixed partition also trains 1.5x faster per step than dense attention with FlashAttention, though both use more memory; a ViT on a downsampled input loses half its mean average precision. Hard exclusive assignment is the only region assignment we tested that is both stable and most accurate: softmax and Sinkhorn relaxations diverge, and Gumbel-softmax trains but is less accurate. We also report the limits: a ResNet-18 is more accurate on every task we trained it on in this from-scratch regime, and anchors train faster than FlashAttention only from about 1536x1536 pixels and never use less memory.
authors: Aadi Gupta

title: Mixture of Latent Recursions for Low-Rank Adaptation
abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) performs task-specific adaptation using a fixed low-rank architecture, whose expressiveness is typically increased by enlarging or adding learnable modules with a proportional parameter overhead. We introduce Mixture of Latent Recursions (MoLR), an adaptive recursion framework that enhances adaptation expressiveness while preserving parameter efficiency. MoLR recursively refines the down-projected latent representation of each input using a shared transformation. A lightweight threshold-based router independently determines whether each token should undergo further refinement, while dynamically adjusted thresholds encourage balanced utilization across recursion depths. Extensive experiments across diverse language and vision tasks demonstrate that MoLR consistently outperforms representative LoRA variants with negligible parameter overhead over LoRA. Further analyses show that MoLR learns input-dependent recursion-depth allocation and enables a controllable inference-time compute-performance trade-off without requiring retraining. Code will be publicly available.
authors: Weixun Luo, Ye Mao, Ranran Huang

title: Sampling non-abelian lattice gauge theories with diffusion models
abstract: We present gauge-equivariant diffusion models as samplers for lattice gauge theories (LGTs).
